hiv-aids-first-reports-1981.summary: In 1981 the CDC reported a rare pneumonia in five young men, the first sign of AIDS; it has since killed at least 42.3 million people. Its first clinical report, on June 5, described five cases: previously healthy gay men, one reporting injecting drug use, in whom Pneumocystis pneumonia, an infection seen only in people with wrecked immune systems, had appeared without known cause. Cases of Kaposi’s sarcoma, a rare skin cancer, followed, and CDC formed a task force to monitor the outbreak. Its cause, a retrovirus later named HIV that attacks immune cells, was identified by Robert Gallo’s and Luc Montagnier’s groups in 1983.

hiv-aids-first-reports-1981.detail: HIV had crossed from other primates to humans in west-central Africa decades earlier. Antiretroviral treatment now makes HIV infection a manageable chronic condition, and 40.9 million people were living with it in 2025.

hyatt-regency-walkway-collapse-1981.summary: In July 1981 two walkways in a Kansas City hotel fell on a dance and killed 114 people; a changed rod detail doubled the load on one nut. About 1,600 people were there for a Friday tea dance; 114 died and 216 were injured. Original drawings carried both walkways on single continuous rods, but fabricator Havens Steel proposed two offset sets of rods instead, which made the fourth-floor box beams carry both walkways, with 30 percent of the strength needed. That disaster, America’s deadliest accidental structural failure since 1860, reshaped engineering ethics and emergency management.

hyatt-regency-walkway-collapse-1981.detail: Each walkway was 120 feet long and weighed 64,000 pounds; its fourth-floor bridge hung directly above its second-floor bridge. Engineer Daniel Duncan of Jack D. Gillum and Associates accepted that rod change by telephone without calculations. Investigators found the structure would have failed under one third of that night’s load, and Gillum’s firm lost its licenses in four states.

ibm-pc-1981.summary: In August 1981 IBM launched its Personal Computer at $1,565, and the computer became standard office equipment. IBM's cheapest computer two weeks earlier had cost $10,000; Tandy, Commodore and Apple then owned personal computing. It cost $1,565 with 16 KB of RAM, a Color Graphics Adapter and keyboard, with no disk drives; IBM’s cheapest computer two weeks earlier had cost $10,000. Tandy, Commodore and Apple then owned personal computing, and IBM was known for slow, bureaucratic business systems. William Lowe and Don Estridge’s Boca Raton team, code-named Project Chess, built it in one year from off-the-shelf parts around Intel’s 8088 processor, with open architecture so dealers could repair it and outsiders could add cards and software. PC compatibles became computing’s de facto standard.

ibm-pc-1981.detail: Rivals reverse-engineered the PC’s BIOS, and Columbia Data Products shipped a legal clone in June 1982. By 1985, 56 percent of American companies with personal computers used IBM PCs or compatibles. IBM sold its PC business to Lenovo in 2004.

infosys-founded-1981.summary: In 1981 seven engineers founded Infosys in Pune with $250; India's software export industry grew from such firms. It moved to Bangalore in 1983 and briefly made hardware such as telex machines before its core business, writing custom software offshore for overseas clients, took off after India’s economic liberalisation of 1991. Infosys listed on Bombay Stock Exchange in 1993 and in March 1999 became the first Indian company on Nasdaq, then among that market’s top 20 by value.

infosys-founded-1981.detail: The six co-founders were Nandan Nilekani, Kris Gopalakrishnan, S. D. Shibulal, K. Dinesh, N. S. Raghavan and Ashok Arora. Infosys is counted among India’s Big Six IT companies, and its Mysore campus, called the world’s largest corporate university, trains up to 14,000 recruits at once.

ms-dos-1981.summary: In August 1981 IBM shipped its PC with MS-DOS, which Microsoft had bought for $75,000; Microsoft kept the right to sell it to others. Microsoft had no operating system of its own: it hired Tim Paterson in May 1981 and that July paid Seattle Computer Products $25,000 for his 86-DOS, which he had written in six weeks as a clone of Digital Research’s CP/M for Intel’s 8086 chip. MS-DOS was built in modules, with device drivers that any 8086-family computer maker could adapt, and within one year Microsoft had licensed it to over 70 other companies.

ms-dos-1981.detail: MS-DOS ran IBM PC compatibles throughout the 1980s and carried Microsoft from programming-language vendor to platform owner. It parted ways with IBM’s PC DOS in 1993.

mtv-launch-1981.summary: In August 1981 MTV began playing music videos all day; the look of a song started to matter as much as its sound. It grew out of Warner Cable’s experimental QUBE operation in Columbus, Ohio, whose PopClips program had tested music videos on television. MTV ran videos around the clock, introduced by on-air hosts called video jockeys, and sent its feed by satellite to cable systems nationwide. Its rock format kept most Black artists off air until Michael Jackson’s “Billie Jean” broke through in 1983.

mtv-launch-1981.detail: Warner spun MTV into MTV Networks in 1984, and Viacom bought control in 1985 and 1986. After four decades MTV had shifted from music to reality programming for young adults, reaching 67 million American homes in 2023, down from 99 million at its 2011 peak.

nasal-cpap-sleep-apnoea-sydney-1981.summary: On 18 April 1981 Colin Sullivan, Michael Berthon-Jones, Faiq Issa and Lorraine Eves reported that air delivered through a nasal mask at low pressure held open airways of five patients with severe obstructive sleep apnoea, abolishing apnoeas and restoring sleep. Previously tracheostomy was main effective treatment. Their first devices used a vacuum-cleaner motor and masks glued to patients' faces. A 1983 paper extended use to obesity-hypoventilation, and a five-year follow-up confirmed home use. Sullivan's patents were licensed to Baxter and then to ResMed, founded in Sydney in 1989 by Peter Farrell, which became a global supplier. CPAP remains standard therapy for a condition affecting hundreds of millions.

nmt-1981.summary: In October 1981 Nordic Mobile Telephone opened in Sweden, with Norway following on 10 November, after an NMT network began in Saudi Arabia on 1 September; roaming across borders came with it, and Nokia grew on it. Nordic telecommunications administrations had specified this automatic analog cellular system jointly. It answered congestion on those countries’ manual car-telephone networks. Its specifications were free and open, so many companies built NMT equipment and prices fell, which proved decisive for Ericsson and for Nokia, then Mobira. By 1985 NMT had 110,000 subscribers, the world’s largest mobile network, and its roaming across borders and its open standard shaped GSM, which later replaced it.

nmt-1981.detail: Early NMT phones were mounted in car trunks with handset and display beside the driver. Its first version used 450 MHz, and its 900 MHz variant with more channels came in 1986.

oil-palm-weevil-malaysia-1981.summary: Malaysian plantations in 1970s pay thousands of workers to dust oil palm flowers with pollen by hand because African oil palm fruit sets poorly in Southeast Asia. Entomologist Rahman Anwar Syed, working for Unilever in Cameroon, shows in 1979 that weevils of genus Elaeidobius, not wind, pollinate African palms. After quarantine tests Malaysia releases E. kamerunicus at estates in February 1981; it spreads across peninsula and Borneo within a year and reaches Indonesia in 1983. Fruit set and kernel yield rise sharply and hand pollination ends, lowering costs for an industry that by 2020 supplies most of world palm oil from Indonesia and Malaysia.

osirak-reactor-strike-1981.summary: France had agreed in 1975 to sell Iraq a 70-megawatt materials-testing reactor, Osiris-type, fuelled with highly enriched uranium, built at Tuwaitha near Baghdad as Tammuz-1 and known abroad as Osirak. Iran bombed it lightly in September 1980. On 7 June 1981 eight Israeli F-16s escorted by F-15s fly 1,100 kilometres through Jordanian and Saudi airspace and drop sixteen 1,000-kilogram bombs, collapsing its dome weeks before planned start-up; one French technician dies. UN Security Council Resolution 487 condemns Israel and Reagan's administration briefly suspends aircraft deliveries. Analysts dispute whether this delayed or spurred Saddam Hussein's clandestine enrichment programme uncovered after 1991; Israel repeats such a strike on Syria's al-Kibar site in 2007.

sts-1-space-shuttle-1981.summary: In April 1981 Columbia flew the first Space Shuttle mission, America’s first crewed spaceflight since Apollo–Soyuz in 1975. Commander John Young, on his fifth flight, and pilot Robert Crippen rode NASA's first crewed launch on solid-fuel boosters and the first American crewed vehicle flown without a prior uncrewed powered test. Columbia met all 113 test objectives and opened 30 years of shuttle flights.

'STS-1', NASA (2025)

sts-1-space-shuttle-1981.detail: A computer timing fault had scrubbed its launch two days earlier, so by coincidence Columbia flew 20 years to the day after Yuri Gagarin’s Vostok 1. It had spent 610 days in processing while its heat-shield tiles were replaced. Carrying only flight instrumentation, it fired its de-orbit engines on its 36th orbit and glided to Edwards Air Force Base on April 14 after 54.5 hours.

picture.credit: NASA Johnson Space Center, public domain, via NASA Image and Video Library

blade-runner-1982.summary: In 1982 Blade Runner put artificial people indistinguishable from humans on screen and asked what the difference was. Adapted from Philip K. Dick’s 1968 novel Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?, it is set in a rain-soaked Los Angeles of 2019 where Tyrell Corporation bio-engineers replicants, synthetic humans built with four-year lifespans to labor on space colonies. When four led by Roy Batty escape to Earth, former police officer Rick Deckard is recalled to hunt and “retire” them. Seven versions exist, and it entered the National Film Registry in 1993 as a foundational work of cyberpunk.

blade-runner-1982.detail: The film took $6.1 million its opening weekend but underperformed against E.T. and Star Trek II and split critics over its slow pace. Scott’s director’s cut of 1992 and Final Cut of 2007 fed a cult following.

commodore-64-1982.summary: In 1982 the Commodore 64 went on sale at $595; it became the best-selling single computer model ever, with some 12 to 17 million sold. Its MOS Technology subsidiary had designed its VIC-II graphics and SID sound chips in 1981 for a game console, and a small team built a computer around them over Thanksgiving and Christmas weekends. Because Commodore made its own chips, each unit cost about $135 to build, and it sold through ordinary retail stores rather than computer shops. Guinness World Records lists it as the best-selling desktop computer ever, with estimates of 12.5 to 17 million sold.

compact-disc-1982.summary: In October 1982 the first compact discs went on sale in Japan; music became digital data, and vinyl sales fell for 25 years. Philips and Sony co-developed the format and set it down in 1980 in their Red Book standard: stereo sound sampled 44,100 times a second at 16 bits, stored as microscopic pits along a spiral track in a 120 mm polycarbonate disc and read by laser, so nothing touches its surface and copies do not wear. CDs outsold vinyl and cassettes in America by 1991, and CD-ROM carried CDs into computing before downloads and streaming ended their reign.

compact-disc-1982.detail: A disc held 74 minutes of music or about 650 MiB of data. Philips lore credits Sony’s Norio Ohga with insisting on room for Beethoven’s Ninth, a story Philips engineer Kees Immink calls myth. CDs held 92.3 percent of America’s music market in 2000, and over 200 billion discs had been sold by 2007.

cyberspace-burning-chrome-1982.summary: In 1982 William Gibson's story Burning Chrome coined cyberspace for a networked space of data, before such a space existed. He had read it to four people at a Denver science fiction convention in autumn 1981, Bruce Sterling among them. Its narrator, hardware expert Automatic Jack, and his partner Bobby Quine, “console cowboy,” break into a crime boss’s systems through cyberspace, which Gibson describes as graphic “consensual hallucination” shared across computer networks. Oxford English Dictionary says this word was “Apparently coined by William Gibson” and cites this story, though Danish artist Susanne Ussing and architect Carsten Hoff had exhibited as Atelier Cyberspace in the late 1960s.

dragon-systems-founded-1982.summary: In 1982 James and Janet Baker founded Dragon Systems to sell speech recognition built on statistics. James had described a speech understanding system called DRAGON in 1975; he served as president while she was chief executive. Their DragonDictate for DOS used hidden Markov models, which score the likelihood that a stretch of sound matches each word, but 1980s hardware could not find word boundaries, so users paused after every word. In 1997 Dragon NaturallySpeaking 1.0 became their first continuous dictation product.

dragon-systems-founded-1982.detail: The Bakers sold Dragon to Belgium’s Lernout & Hauspie in June 2000 in an all-stock deal. That company collapsed in fraud five months later, wiping out their payment and prompting their lawsuit against Goldman Sachs. Dragon passed to Nuance and, in 2022, to Microsoft.

fifth-generation-project-1982.summary: In 1982 Japan launched a ten-year national project to build intelligent computers, which alarmed the West and ended short of its goals. The Ministry of International Trade and Industry planned machines built on massively parallel hardware and logic programming. Japan had followed American and British leads through four generations of hardware, from vacuum tubes to microprocessors; MITI now sought an “epoch-making computer” for knowledge processing, and set up Institute for New Generation Computer Technology, ICOT, with Japan’s computer makers. The project ran until 1994, spent just under ¥57 billion, about $320 million, advanced concurrent logic programming and ended in commercial failure.

fifth-generation-project-1982.detail: ICOT built machines running its concurrent logic language KL1, aiming at 100 million to one billion logical inferences per second over large knowledge bases. Alarmed rivals founded America’s Strategic Computing Initiative and MCC, Britain’s Alvey and Europe’s ESPRIT.

helicobacter-pylori-culture-perth-1982.summary: Pathologist Robin Warren had observed curved bacteria on inflamed gastric mucosa since 1979. With registrar Barry Marshall he set out to culture them; after months of failure, plates left over Easter 1982 grew colonies. Their 1983 Lancet letters and 1984 paper linked bacteria to gastritis and peptic ulcers, challenging doctrine that stomach acidity made ulcers a stress disorder. Marshall drank a culture in 1984 and developed gastritis. Antibiotic eradication became standard, cutting ulcer surgery and later gastric cancer rates, and in 2005 Nobel Assembly awarded them Physiology or Medicine prize. Year follows culture date; publication came in 1983 and 1984.

sources.qualifies: Primary letters

sources.qualifies: Primary paper

hopfield-network-1982.summary: In 1982 Hopfield showed a network of simple units could store and recall memories like a physicist's spin glass. His network has a single layer in which every neuron connects to every other with symmetric weights. Patterns are stored by strengthening connections between neurons active together; to recall one, you fix some inputs and let the network settle toward its energy function’s minimum, which recovers that whole stored pattern from partial or noisy cues. It became neural network research’s standard model, and in 2024 Hopfield shared the Nobel Prize in Physics with Geoffrey Hinton.

Hopfield, J. J., 'Neural Networks and Physical Systems with Emergent Collective Computational Abilities', Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 79, no. 8 (1982): 2554-2558
sources.author: Hopfield, J. J.
sources.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
sources.confirms: Hopfield's 1982 paper shows that a system of many simple neuron-like units produces a content-addressable memory that recovers a whole stored pattern from a sufficient part of it.

sources.author: Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences
sources.confirms: John Hopfield discovered in 1982 an associative memory, the Hopfield network, that stores patterns and recreates them from distorted input, using an energy picture borrowed from the physics of atomic spins.

hopfield-network-1982.detail: Hopfield acknowledged earlier work by Rosenblatt, Nakano, Amari and William Little, who had proposed modifying Ising’s magnet model by Hebbian learning. Hopfield applied the newly developed Sherrington–Kirkpatrick spin-glass theory to such networks with binary neurons. His 1984 paper extended the model to continuous neurons.

picture.credit: bhadeshia123, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

humulin-recombinant-insulin-1982.summary: In 1982 Eli Lilly began selling human insulin made by engineered bacteria, the first genetically engineered drug. Genentech developed its production technique but did not sell it; Eli Lilly marketed Humulin in 1982. Until then insulin came from pig and cow pancreases, and about 2 percent of patients had allergic reactions, mostly to preservatives. Humulin was the first medication made by inserting human DNA into a host cell, here the bacterium E. coli, which grows and reproduces normally while producing a synthetic version of human insulin, freeing supply from slaughterhouses.

sources.confirms: Describes production of human insulin in E. coli from Genentech's synthetic genes and Lilly's clinical development leading to approval in 1982, the first recombinant DNA drug.

sources.confirms: Humulin, approved by the FDA in 1982, was the first recombinant human insulin marketed, replacing animal-derived insulin.

humulin-recombinant-insulin-1982.detail: By 2002 about 70 percent of insulin sold worldwide was recombinant human insulin, though clinical evidence on whether it causes fewer allergic reactions remains conflicting.

kenya-ceramic-jiko-1982.summary: From 1982 Max Kinyanjui and partners in Nairobi redesigned Kenya's standard metal charcoal stove by fitting a fired clay liner inside a sheet-metal case, insulated with a layer of cement and vermiculite. Hugh Allen's manual records that this Kenya Ceramic Jiko burns 25 to 40 percent less charcoal than traditional all-metal stoves. Informal-sector metalworkers and potters produced it in volume, and a World Bank-supported programme helped standardise liners and train makers. Within a decade the stove was in a large share of urban Kenyan households and was copied across East Africa. Daniel Kammen later cited it as evidence that improved stoves succeed when local producers, not only donors, shape design and distribution.

sources.author: Allen, Hugh
sources.confirms: Charcoal stove with ceramic liner in a metal case; burns 25 to 40 percent less charcoal than traditional stoves

kenya-ceramic-jiko-1982.detail: Littlewood and Holt's case study credits Kinyanjui with introducing ceramic jikos in Kenya and dates his stove design work to 1982 with World Bank backing. Allen's 1991 manual for stovemakers documents construction and fuel savings. Kammen's Scientific American article (July 1995) placed the jiko in a global cookstove debate about fuel use, indoor smoke and deforestation. Allen's manual, published for Practical Action in 1991, remains a reference for liner moulds and firing.

mcc-consortium-1983.summary: In 1983 American computer firms pooled research in MCC to answer Japan's Fifth Generation project, announced that year, which many American and European firms read as a bid to control high-end computing; such pooling was illegal until Congress passed its National Cooperative Research Act in 1984. Admiral Bobby Ray Inman, former National Security Agency director and CIA deputy director, led it. MCC became the first and for a time largest such consortium in America, and voted to dissolve in June 2000.

mcc-consortium-1983.detail: Austin, Texas, beat Atlanta, Research Triangle, Washington and Stanford in 1983 after University of Texas offered land and a building and Ross Perot lent his plane for recruiting. MCC, reportedly the largest customer of Symbolics and Lisp Machines, took no government money for years.

te-kohanga-reo-1982.summary: By 1970s fewer than 5 percent of Maori children spoke te reo Maori, and a 1979 Department of Maori Affairs hui on language loss proposed immersing preschoolers with fluent kaumatua (elders). First kohanga reo opened at Pukeatua in Wainuiomata in April 1982, run by whanau on marae principles; within a year more than 100 operated and by 1993 over 800 enrolled some 14,000 children. Kohanga reo led to kura kaupapa Maori immersion primary schools from 1985 and whare wananga tertiary institutions. Te Kohanga Reo National Trust runs movement. Language-nest model was adopted in Hawai'i (Punana Leo, 1984) and by Indigenous communities worldwide.

te-kohanga-reo-1982.detail: King's chapter in The Green Book of Language Revitalization places kohanga reo among most successful revitalisation efforts. Hohepa, Smith, Smith and McNaughton studied language interaction inside kohanga; Tangaere describes it as whanau development as much as language teaching. Funding disputes with government and a 2012 Waitangi Tribunal claim over Crown underfunding followed. Te reo Maori became an official language in 1987; speaker numbers stabilised but remain a minority of Maori.

amps-1983.summary: In October 1983 the first American cellular service opened in Chicago; car phones became a product anyone could buy. Bell Labs had developed AMPS from 1968, refined it with Motorola, and run equipment tests in Chicago with about 100 units since 1978. In AMPS, cell centers assign radio channels to handsets by signal strength, so one frequency can be reused in cells far enough apart, letting far more phones share a city’s spectrum than earlier mobile systems allowed. Analog AMPS remained North America’s main mobile system through the 1980s into the 2000s.

sources.title: Advanced Mobile Phone System (Wikipedia)
Cellular network (Wikipedia)

sources.author: Young, W. R.

amps-1983.detail: Motorola’s DynaTAC 8000x, history's first hand-carried cellular phone, arrived in 1983. AMPS was open to static and to eavesdropping by scanner, but it spread to Israel, Australia, Singapore and Pakistan and carried IBM’s Simon, the first smartphone, in 1992. American carriers were released from supporting it in 2008.

apple-lisa-1983.summary: In January 1983 Apple's Lisa brought windows and a mouse to market at $9,995; it flopped, and the Macintosh took its ideas a year later at $2,495. Begun in 1978 as successor to Apple II, Lisa changed course after Steve Jobs saw Xerox PARC’s mouse-driven Alto in 1979, demonstrations Apple obtained by selling Xerox stock. Built on Motorola’s 68000 processor, Lisa offered windows and mouse, document-centered workflow, protected memory and preloaded office software, years before such features reached IBM’s PC. Reviewers admired its technology but balked at its workstation price, and Lisa sold an estimated 10,000 to 60,000 units in two years.

sources.title: Apple Lisa - Wikipedia
Hsu, Hansen, 'The Lisa: Apple's Most Influential Failure', CHM blog (2023)
sources.author: Hsu, Hansen
sources.confirms: The page says Lisa was released to the public on January 19, 1983 for $9,995, incorporated Xerox PARC GUI ideas, used a document-centric workflow, and was a key influence on the Macintosh, which shipped for $2,495 in January 1984.
sources.qualifies: The source gives the Macintosh price as $2,495 but does not describe it as a quarter of Lisa’s price.

sources.title: Edwards, Benj, '30 years of the Apple Lisa and the Apple IIe', Macworld (2013)
sources.author: Edwards, Benj

sources.qualifies: The source says the Macintosh followed Lisa by one year, not that it took Lisa’s ideas “for a quarter.”

apple-lisa-1983.verification_note: Sources say the Macintosh followed Lisa by one year at $2,495 without describing that as a quarter of Lisa's price.
apple-lisa-1983.detail: Reviewers also faulted Lisa’s scarce third-party software and its unreliable “Twiggy” floppy drives. Jobs, forced off Lisa in 1980, had taken over Macintosh and remade it as cheaper Lisa; its arrival in 1984 finished Lisa.

dectalk-1983.summary: In December 1983 DEC announced DECtalk, which turned typed text into nine adjustable voices; Stephen Hawking spoke through it for decades and became identified with its voice. Klatt’s source-filter algorithm, known as KlattTalk or MITalk, models speech as a sound source shaped by a filter standing in for the human vocal tract. Delivered from early 1984, its voices ran from default Perfect Paul to Whispering Wendy, each adjustable by parameters such as throat size, and it gave voice to public systems and to people unable to speak.

sources.author: Pisoni, David B., et al.
sources.confirms: DECtalk is a stand-alone commercial text-to-speech system from Digital Equipment Corporation whose prototype, Klattalk, grew from Klatt's 1980 formant synthesiser.

sources.author: PubMed Central
sources.confirms: MITalk's architecture served as the basis for several commercial text-to-speech systems, as Klatt's 1987 review records.

dectalk-1983.detail: Perfect Paul announced station identifications on NOAA Weather Radio in the late 1990s, and Huge Harry still reads airport weather broadcasts.

dns-1983.summary: In 1983 Paul Mockapetris created the Domain Name System so names could replace numbers; the internet could grow without a central list. Until then every ARPANET computer looked up names in HOSTS.TXT, a single text file maintained at Stanford Research Institute by Elizabeth Feinler, and keeping that central table current had become slow and unwieldy. DNS is hierarchical and distributed: authoritative name servers answer for each domain and can delegate subdomains to other servers, so no single database holds everything, and it translates memorable names into numerical IP addresses machines need.

sources.author: Mockapetris, Paul; Dunlap, Kevin J.

dns-1983.detail: HOSTS.TXT had strained by the early 1980s. Jon Postel had asked Mockapetris to reconcile five competing proposals; he designed DNS instead. Four Berkeley students wrote BIND, its first Unix implementation, in 1984, and DNS now underpins cloud services and content delivery networks.

egypt-oral-rehydration-ncddp-1983.summary: Egypt's Ministry of Health, with USAID funding, scales a National Control of Diarrheal Diseases Project nationwide from 1983 after pilots in 1981 and 1982. Locally packaged oral rehydration salts go on sale in pharmacies and village shops at a subsidised price, television dramas and spots teach mothers to mix and give solution, and physicians are retrained away from drips and antidiarrhoeals. Surveys show use of ORS in diarrhoea episodes rising from near zero to about half within five years. Infant mortality falls by roughly a third between 1982 and 1987 and deaths attributed to diarrhoea drop far more, with programme evaluations crediting some 300,000 averted child deaths. It becomes a reference case for mass health communication in middle-income countries.

egypt-oral-rehydration-ncddp-1983.detail: Programme evaluators attributed mortality decline to ORS use in 1990, and a full evaluation followed in 1995. Rashad's demographic reappraisal argues part of that decline would have occurred anyway.

esprit-1983.summary: In 1983 Europe launched ESPRIT, a shared research programme in information technology, to catch up with America and Japan. It was Europe’s answer, alongside Britain’s Alvey, to Japan’s Fifth Generation push. In late 1981, industry commissioner Étienne Davignon invited heads of Europe’s twelve largest IT companies to round-table talks; after a 1983 pilot phase, research ministers approved ESPRIT in February 1984 with 1.5 billion ECU over four years, half from the Community and half from participants. It produced no European IBM, but it built a cross-border research community, and today’s Horizon Europe descends from it.

esprit-1983.detail: ESPRIT’s principle was pre-competitive research: companies from at least two member states worked together below product level, so no government could kill it by favouring its own champion. Its projects included transputer-based parallel computers, the CGAL geometry library and the BBC Domesday Project.

famicom-nes-1983.summary: In July 1983 Nintendo released its Famicom in Japan; it revived a crashed games industry and made Mario a household name. President Hiroshi Yamauchi had asked for a simple, cheap machine that could run arcade games from cartridges; engineer Masayuki Uemura built its 8-bit hardware on that of Donkey Kong. For America, where 1983’s crash had soured stores on video games, Lance Barr and Don James restyled it as the Nintendo Entertainment System. It gave Nintendo near-monopoly in Japan and North America, sold 61.91 million units and made licensing third-party developers under strict terms the console industry’s standard business model.

famicom-nes-1983.detail: Uemura reused Game & Watch controller designs, and his wife suggested its name. Nintendo styled its NES to resemble a video cassette recorder and bundled it with a light gun and R.O.B., a toy robot. Nintendo tested it in New York from October 18, 1985, and launched it nationwide on September 27, 1986.

feigenbaum-fifth-generation-book-1983.summary: In 1983 Feigenbaum and McCorduck's The Fifth Generation warned that Japan would lead in computing; M. Granger Morgan reviewed it in Journal of Policy Analysis and Management that same year. Their 275-page book, published from Reading, Massachusetts, was priced at $15.35.

franklin-dam-high-court-1983.summary: Tasmania's Hydro-Electric Commission planned a dam on Gordon River below Franklin to add 180 megawatts. Opposition led by Bob Brown's Tasmanian Wilderness Society mounted a blockade from December 1982 with about 1,200 arrests. After Bob Hawke's Labor government won office in March 1983 promising to halt works, it legislated under external affairs power using World Heritage listing. On 1 July 1983 High Court upheld Commonwealth law four to three in Commonwealth v Tasmania. Dragun's 1983 analysis and Bandler's 1987 paper weigh energy and environmental factors. Decision reshaped federal environmental power and ended large hydro building in Australia.

gnu-project-1983.summary: In September 1983 Stallman announced GNU, a free operating system anyone could change and share. Years earlier, at MIT’s AI Lab, a new printer’s proprietary firmware had stopped him fixing its software, which convinced him that non-free software was a social problem. GNU, recursive acronym for “GNU’s not Unix,” would grant everyone rights to run, copy, distribute, study and modify every part of their computers’ software. Linus Torvalds’s Linux kernel, released under GNU’s GPLv2 in 1992, completed GNU/Linux, an operating system made entirely of free software.

gnu-project-1983.detail: Those rights were to cover software from the kernel to the utilities. Stallman chose Unix as his model because it was portable and “fairly clean,” though he had never used it. By June 1987 his project had produced GNU Emacs, its almost finished C compiler, GCC, and many utilities, and his GNU Manifesto’s four freedoms defined free software. GNU’s own kernel, Hurd, stayed unfinished.

grameen-bank-1983.summary: In 1983 Bangladesh chartered Grameen Bank to lend tiny sums to poor women without collateral. During Bangladesh’s 1974 famine, Muhammad Yunus, an economics professor at University of Chittagong, lent $27 of his own money to 42 villagers, mostly bamboo stool makers, so they could buy materials without predatory moneylenders. Grameen, Bengali for “village,” lends through solidarity lending, in which borrowers form groups that back one another. By 2005 it had lent over $4.7 billion, and in 2006 the bank and Yunus shared the Nobel Peace Prize.

sources.confirms: Yunus lent US $27 to 42 villagers in Jobra during the 1974 famine and in 1983 succeeded in creating a separate bank for the poor, Grameen Bank, which lends collateral-free, 97 percent to women.

grameen-bank-1983.detail: From 1976 Yunus tested his method in Jobra village with Janata Bank, and it spread over two years. Every borrower recites Grameen’s Sixteen Decisions on social habits. Bankers from Chicago’s ShoreBank helped Yunus incorporate the bank under a Ford Foundation grant, and Grameen America had 19 branches by 2017.

insat-1b-1983.summary: Launched from Space Shuttle Challenger on 30 August 1983 and built by Ford Aerospace to Indian specifications, INSAT-1B nearly fails when its solar array sticks; controllers free it in mid September and position it at 74 degrees east, replacing INSAT-1A lost in 1982. From October 1983 it carries 4,375 two-way voice circuits, relays Doordarshan's national programme to new low-power transmitters across India, broadcasts direct to community sets in villages, and returns about 36,000 weather images from its radiometer before operations end around 1990. Saraf's Nature note sets out this multipurpose design. Later INSAT satellites built by ISRO carry on this combined model.

picture.credit: NASA

jet-tokamak-1983.summary: In June 1983 Europe's JET tokamak made its first plasma at Culham; the largest tokamak for 40 years, it set the fusion power record. Euratom’s member states had chosen Culham in 1977 and approved funding in April 1978 after Soviet tokamak results of 1968 had sent researchers worldwide down that path. A tokamak holds a ring of plasma hotter than our Sun’s core inside magnetic fields. In 1997 JET produced 16 MW of fusion power for 24 MW of heating, the closest approach yet to breakeven, and it shaped ITER’s design.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Joint European Torus
EUROfusion, 'JET', device page
sources.author: EUROfusion
sources.confirms: JET at Culham began its first experimental campaign on 25 June 1983 and made its final pulse on 18 December 2023.

sources.author: Paul-Henri Rebut

sources.confirms: Contemporary technical report on JET's installation at Culham and its first results after the 1983 start of operation; Crossref metadata confirmed.

jet-tokamak-1983.detail: JET was larger than any comparable machine when designed and added external heating. From 1991 to 1993 it added a divertor to remove waste from its plasma, and in 1991 it became the first reactor to burn a 50–50 deuterium-tritium mix. It produced 69.29 megajoules over six seconds in October 2023 and ceased operations that December after 105,842 pulses.

kal-007-gps-civilian-1983.summary: In September 1983 a Soviet fighter shot down a Korean airliner that had strayed off course and 269 died; Reagan publicised GPS's civilian future. The Boeing 747 was flying from New York to Seoul via Anchorage; investigators for the International Civil Aviation Organization concluded its autopilot had probably stayed in heading mode instead of following its inertial navigation system, so it drifted steadily north of its route and crossed Soviet airspace over Kamchatka and Sakhalin. Afterwards, on 16 September, President Ronald Reagan announced that GPS would be freely available for civilian use once sufficiently developed, as a common good, a policy a 1981 Federal Register notice had already set.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Korean Air Lines Flight 007
Ronald Reagan Presidential Library, 'Global Positioning System for International Civil Use (Post Flight KAL 007 Shoot Down)', archival topic guide
sources.author: Ronald Reagan Presidential Library
sources.confirms: After the 1 September 1983 shootdown Reagan announced on 16 September 1983 that GPS would be made available for civil aviation.

sources.author: Scott Pace et al.

kal-007-gps-civilian-1983.verification_note: RAND's policy history shows a 1981 Federal Register notice had already decided not to exclude civilian GPS use outside US territory; Reagan's 16 September 1983 statement announced that policy dramatically, with availability not expected until 1987 or 1988.
kal-007-gps-civilian-1983.detail: Its 246 passengers and 23 crew included United States Congressman Larry McDonald. Soviet air defences treated KAL 007 as an intruding American spy plane, denied knowledge of its shootdown, then claimed it was on an espionage mission. America also altered tracking for aircraft leaving Alaska.

leontief-horses-1983.summary: In 1983 Wassily Leontief warned that computers could do to workers what tractors did to horses, reducing labor’s role in production. Nineteenth-century technology, he wrote, had strengthened labor’s dominant role, so competitive pricing spread growth’s gains widely; new technology was reversing that. Humans, unlike horses, can control their government, so he proposed remedies from unemployment relief to Swedish-style income policies in rich countries, and public works in poorer ones.

sources.title: 1983 TechnologicalAdvanceEconomicGro
Wassily Leontief, 'Technological Advance, Economic Growth, and the Distribution of Income', Population and Development Review 9 (1983)

sources.confirms: The September 1983 article in which Leontief argues that computers and robots progressively reduce labour's role in production, the context of his horse comparison.

leontief-horses-1983.detail: Leontief called this comparison “a somewhat shocking but essentially appropriate analogy” in his paper. Horses willing to accept smaller rations of oats, he noted, would only have slowed their elimination by ever better tractors: “If horses had controlled the government, this would have been a quite different story.”

maruti-800-launch-1983.summary: On 14 December 1983 Maruti Udyog, a joint venture between Government of India and Suzuki, handed over first Maruti 800, a 796 cc hatchback based on Suzuki Alto, at its Gurgaon plant. Indian car output had been frozen for decades around Ambassador and Padmini designs. Maruti brought Japanese production methods, supplier development and quality standards, and within a decade held over half of Indian car market. Its component supplier base around Delhi and later Suzuki's Manesar plant made India a small car export hub. Over 2.7 million Maruti 800s were built before production ended in 2014.

sources.title: Anthony P. D'Costa, 'The restructuring of the Indian automobile industry: Indian state and Japanese capital', World Development 23 (1995)
sources.author: Anthony P. D'Costa
sources.confirms: Maruti Suzuki venture and restructuring of Indian car industry

sources.title: Maruti Suzuki India, 'Company history'
sources.confirms: 1983 launch of Maruti 800 from Gurgaon

maruti-800-launch-1983.verification_note: D'Costa abstract confirmed. Exact handover date from company and press histories; production totals are approximate.
maruti-800-launch-1983.detail: D'Costa's World Development article analyses Maruti Suzuki collaboration as a case of state-led industrial restructuring with Japanese organisational practices. Company and press histories give 14 December 1983 handover to Harpal Singh. Market share figures vary by year.

picture.alt: An early Maruti 800 hatchback parked on a street in Goa
picture.credit: Polytope4d

metcalfes-law-1983.summary: In 1983 Metcalfe told 3Com's sales force a network's value grows with its users squared. His slide showed network cost rising in step with device count while network value rose with its square, since N devices can form N × (N − 1) connections; below critical mass, networks cost more than they were worth, and above it, as Metcalfe put it, “the sky’s the limit.” George Gilder named it Metcalfe’s law in Forbes in September 1993, and it became network effects’ standard account for Internet, web and social networks.

sources.title: Metcalfe's law
Metcalfe's Law after 40 Years of Ethernet
Metcalfe, Bob, 'Metcalfe's Law after 40 Years of Ethernet', Computer 46 (2013), pp. 26-31
sources.author: Metcalfe, Robert
sources.confirms: Metcalfe's own retrospective on the law he first presented to 3Com's sales force around 1980, that network value grows with the square of users, and its later critics.

metcalfes-law-1983.detail: 3Com hoped critical mass was about 30 nodes, and salespeople used his slide to push customers’ Ethernets past that threshold. Critics argue network value grows more slowly, nearer n log n.

motorola-dynatac-1983.summary: In March 1983 Motorola unveiled the DynaTAC, the first handheld mobile phone for sale, a 790 gram brick with 30 minutes of talk time. Bell Labs had proposed cellular telephony in 1947, and Motorola’s car phones were so heavy and power-hungry that they ran only with the engine on, until John F. Mitchell and Martin Cooper’s team built a portable prototype and made its first call in 1973. DynaTAC cost $3,995, over 1,192 hours of work at America’s minimum wage, so it never became a mass-market item.

sources.author: Smithsonian Institution

sources.qualifies: Dates production to 1984, a year after the 1983 unveiling.

motorola-dynatac-1983.detail: That 1973 first call reportedly went to a wrong number. DynaTAC, short for “Dynamic Adaptive Total Area Coverage,” took ten hours to charge for 30 minutes of talk and stored 30 numbers behind an LED display. Motorola sold DynaTAC models until 1994; its far smaller MicroTAC superseded them from 1989.

picture.alt: Martin Cooper holds a DynaTAC prototype from 1973 at e21 Forum in Taipei in 2007.

national-programme-improved-chulhas-1983.summary: Department of Non-Conventional Energy Sources launches a demonstration project for improved cookstoves in 1983, made national in April 1985 to save fuelwood, slow deforestation and cut smoke in kitchens. Mud and ceramic stoves with chimneys, built by trained village workers under subsidy, number about 12 million by March 1992 and over 30 million by 2000. Surveys find many cracked, abandoned or altered within a year or two: designs ignore cooking habits and subsidies reward installation counts instead of use. A 2002 assessment concludes dissemination targets crowded out quality, and central funding stops that year. Later cookstove schemes and Ujjwala's LPG push in 2016 draw lessons from this programme.

sources.title: V. V. N. Kishore and P. V. Ramana, 'Improved cookstoves in rural India: how improved are they? A critique of the National Programme on Improved Chulhas (NPIC)', Energy 27 (2002) 47-63

national-programme-improved-chulhas-1983.detail: FAO's 1993 compendium gives 1983 pilot, April 1985 national programme, 12 million by March 1992 and fuel savings estimates. Total above 30 million comes from that 2002 assessment and MNRE statistics.

picture.alt: A traditional mud chulha burning wood outdoors in rural Tamil Nadu, the stove type the programme set out to replace
picture.credit: mckaysavage

osborne-effect-1983.summary: In September 1983 Osborne Computer went bankrupt after announcing its next portables too early. Months earlier, founder Adam Osborne had pre-announced its Osborne Executive and Osborne Vixen, then only prototypes, as successors to its Osborne 1 portable of 1981. When Osborne toured dealers from 17 April, in his words, “All of them just cancelled their orders for the Osborne 1.” He slashed prices to raise cash; for months sales were practically nonexistent. The collapse gave its name to the Osborne effect, in which customers cancel or defer orders for a current product once a replacement is announced too soon.

sources.title: Osborne effect - Wikipedia
Encyclopedia.com, "Osborne, Adam" (Encyclopedia of World Biography)
sources.author: Encyclopedia of World Biography
sources.confirms: Osborne Computer launched the Osborne 1 in 1981 and filed for bankruptcy in September 1983 after pre-announcing successors.

sources.title: Geschichte der Informatik, "Dead End: Osborne"

sources.qualifies: Later analyses attribute the collapse as much to inventory and pricing errors as to the pre-announcement.

osborne-effect-1983.detail: Early in 1983 magazines saw Osborne’s $2,495 Executive in locked hotel rooms under embargo until mid-April, but dealers heard. Former employees dispute that announcements alone sank his company: Kaypro was already selling a machine with a 9-inch screen for $400 less.

pcr-mullis-1983.summary: In 1983 Kary Mullis invented PCR, a way to copy a strand of DNA billions of times. He worked at Cetus Corporation in Emeryville, California, where he synthesised short DNA chains. PCR heats samples to split DNA’s two strands, cools them so short primers bind at each end of its target, and lets polymerase enzymes fill in copies; each cycle doubles that target, so few molecules yield billions. PCR became indispensable to genetic testing, ancient DNA, forensics and pathogen detection, and Mullis shared 1993’s Nobel Prize in Chemistry with Michael Smith.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Polymerase chain reaction
Mullis, K. B., and Faloona, F. A., 'Specific Synthesis of DNA in Vitro via a Polymerase-Catalyzed Chain Reaction', Methods in Enzymology 155 (1987): 335-350
sources.author: Mullis, Kary B.; Faloona, Fred A.
sources.confirms: Mullis and Faloona's methods paper describes the polymerase chain reaction developed at Cetus for exponential amplification of a DNA segment between two primers.

sources.title: Mullis, Kary B., 'Process for Amplifying Nucleic Acid Sequences', US Patent 4,683,202, assigned to Cetus Corp., priority 28 March 1985, granted 28 July 1987
sources.author: Mullis, Kary B.
sources.venue: United States Patent and Trademark Office, via Google Patents
sources.confirms: The PCR patent, with Mullis as sole inventor and Cetus as original assignee, claims a process of cyclic primer extension that amplifies a specific nucleic acid sequence.

pcr-mullis-1983.detail: Mullis has written that his idea came while driving Pacific Coast Highway one night: his method for detecting mutations would instead copy any DNA region through repeated rounds of duplication. Heat-stable Taq polymerase, from Yellowstone hot-spring bacteria, later removed any need to add fresh enzyme every cycle.

picture.alt: Kary Mullis, who devised polymerase chain reaction in 1983, speaking at TED in February 2009
picture.credit: Erik Charlton, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

racter-1984.summary: In 1983 Racter, which generated English prose at random, produced a book, The Policeman's Beard Is Half Constructed, edited by hand. Racter, short for raconteur, was written by William Chamberlain and Thomas Etter to generate English prose at random; Omni had bought its first story, “Soft Ions,” in January 1980 before it existed and funded their work on it. Its text came from a specialized version of Racter, with Chamberlain’s own templates and modules, and was edited from much output. That version was not included in Mindscape’s commercial release of 1984, far simpler BASIC software closer to chatterbots or computerized Mad Libs.

sources.title: Racter
Garcia, Chris, 'Gulliver's Engine', Computer History Museum blog, 28 November 2012
sources.author: Garcia, Chris
sources.confirms: The museum describes Racter as a program that generated English prose and poetry at random, used to write The Policeman's Beard is Half-Constructed, claimed as the first book written by a computer, with its output heavily edited down.

sources.qualifies: Imprint year 1984, not 1983.

racter-1984.detail: PC Magazine found Racter “whimsical and wise and sometimes fun,” and The New York Times wrote in 1985 that it was “on the edge of artificial insanity.”

samsung-64k-dram-1983.summary: In 1983 Samsung announced it would make memory chips and built a 64K DRAM within the year; it is now the largest memory maker on Earth. Samsung Electric Industries had been founded in 1969 as a fertilizer-and-sugar trading group’s manufacturing arm, and in 1974 Samsung had bought Korea Semiconductor as it neared bankruptcy. Within a year of that declaration, Samsung announced it had developed a 64K DRAM, cutting its gap behind first-world chipmakers from over ten years to about four. In 1988 its electronics and semiconductor arms merged into Samsung Electronics, today the world’s largest maker of memory chips.

Samsung Newsroom: history of Samsung Electronics innovation (Korean)
The Dynamics of Samsung's Technological Learning in Semiconductors
sources.author: Kim, Linsu
sources.confirms: Peer-reviewed study of Samsung's 1983 entry into DRAMs, its purchase of Korea Semiconductor in 1974, and its development of a 64K DRAM within a year of the decision.

samsung-64k-dram-1983.detail: Samsung had learned from Japanese partners. Its 64K DRAM used technology licensed from Micron Technology of America for DRAM and from Sharp of Japan for SRAM and ROM.

picture.alt: Samsung 64K DRAM chip of 1983, registered as Korean cultural heritage, photographed by Cultural Heritage Administration.
picture.credit: Cultural Heritage Administration of Korea, Open Government Licence (Korea KOGL Type 1), via Cultural Heritage Administration of Korea (mirrored on Wikimedia Commons)

strategic-computing-initiative-1983.summary: From 1983 the Pentagon spent $1 billion on AI and computing to answer Japan's Fifth Generation project; the AI goals went unmet. Washington read Japan’s project as Sputnik had been read in 1957. SCI was planned like Apollo, with chips, architectures and AI software from many companies and universities meant to combine into machines that would “see, hear, speak, and think like a human.” Its Autonomous Land Vehicle work laid foundations for driverless vehicles.

sources.title: Strategic Computing Initiative
Roland, Alex; Shiman, Philip, Strategic Computing: DARPA and the Quest for Machine Intelligence, 1983-1993 (Cambridge, MA: MIT Press, 2002)
sources.author: Roland, Alex; Shiman, Philip
sources.confirms: The MIT Press history of the Strategic Computing Initiative, a roughly $1 billion DARPA programme from 1983 to 1993 launched in part in response to Japan's Fifth Generation project, whose machine-intelligence goals were not met.
sources.qualifies: Confirmed via the Isis (10.1086/504567) and Technology and Culture (10.1353/tech.2003.0184) reviews, not the book pages.

sources.title: Gray, Chris Hables, review of Roland and Shiman, Strategic Computing, Isis 97, no. 1 (2006), pp. 188-189
sources.author: Gray, Chris Hables
sources.confirms: Peer-reviewed review summarising the programme's 1983 start, Apollo-style planning and unmet AI goals.

strategic-computing-initiative-1983.detail: Britain’s Alvey and the MCC consortium answered Japan likewise. By 1985 SCI had spent $100 million on 92 projects at 60 institutions under Robert Kahn’s early leadership. Jack Schwarz cut its AI funding “deeply and brutally” in 1987, and its DART logistics tool saved billions during Desert Storm.

t-series-cassette-culture-1983.summary: On 11 July 1983 Gulshan Kumar, son of a Delhi fruit juice seller, founds Super Cassettes Industries, later T-Series. Using a Copyright Act clause allowing version recordings of published songs after a fixed royalty, he sells cover versions of film hits, devotional songs and regional music on cassettes priced far below HMV's, through paan shops and street stalls rather than record shops. Cassette players from Southeast Asian grey markets make this possible. Manuel's 1993 study Cassette Culture shows how cheap duplication broke a single label's grip and let hundreds of small producers record local genres. T-Series becomes India's largest label, and after 2018 runs YouTube's most subscribed channel.

sources.title: Peter Manuel, Cassette Culture: Popular Music and Technology in North India (University of Chicago Press, 1993)
sources.author: Peter Manuel
sources.confirms: cassette economics, version recordings, decentralisation of music production, T-Series role

sources.title: Peter Manuel, 'The Cassette Industry and Popular Music in North India', in Popular Music Studies reader (Routledge)
sources.author: Peter Manuel
sources.confirms: cassette industry structure

sources.title: Indian Express, 'From being a fruit juice vendor to becoming the cassette king, Gulshan Kumar's life was no less than a movie'
sources.author: Indian Express
sources.confirms: founding, low prices, devotional catalogue

t-series-cassette-culture-1983.verification_note: Manuel confirmed via publisher page and Crossref; page numbers not cited. Founding date of 11 July 1983 from company and press sources; some profiles give 1983 without a day.
t-series-cassette-culture-1983.detail: Manuel (University of Chicago Press 1993) documents cassette economics, version recordings and regional music boom. Founding date from company history and press profiles. Kumar is murdered in Mumbai in August 1997.

picture.alt: A standard compact audio cassette beside a smaller mini-cassette
picture.credit: Jacek Halicki

tcp-ip-flag-day-1983.summary: On 1 January 1983, the date RFC 801 set for completing its transition, ARPANET switched to TCP/IP, the common protocol that let separate networks join into one internet. Bob Kahn and Vint Cerf had reformulated networking in 1973, publishing in May 1974: a common internetwork protocol would hide differences between local networks, and reliability would move from the network into its hosts, following Louis Pouzin’s CYCLADES. From 1983 Internet Protocol version 4 carried ARPANET’s traffic, letting other networks built on those principles join it, and TCP/IP remains the Internet’s framework.

sources.title: Internet protocol suite - Wikipedia
Cerf, V.; Kahn, R., 'A Protocol for Packet Network Intercommunication', IEEE Transactions on Communications (1974)
sources.author: Cerf, V.; Kahn, R.
sources.confirms: The page presents a protocol for sharing resources across different packet switching networks and says it accommodates variations such as packet sizes, transmission failures, sequencing, and flow control.

sources.qualifies: The RFC sets 1 January 1983 as the planned completion date for the transition, rather than confirming that the ARPANET switched on that day.

tcp-ip-flag-day-1983.verification_note: RFC 801 sets 1 January 1983 as planned completion of NCP-to-TCP/IP transition; accounts of that day's switch come from later histories.
tcp-ip-flag-day-1983.detail: After years of test versions, America’s Department of Defense declared TCP/IP its standard for all military networking in March 1982. A 1985 workshop for 250 vendor representatives pushed TCP/IP into commercial use.

the-day-after-1983.summary: In November 1983 more than 100 million Americans in nearly 39 million households, a 46 rating and 62 percent share, watched The Day After, a film of nuclear war in Kansas; Reagan wrote that it changed his mind on nuclear war policy. It follows families in Lawrence, Kansas, and Kansas City, Missouri, as a NATO–Warsaw Pact clash over Germany escalates into full nuclear exchange, then shows their town in its aftermath. President Ronald Reagan saw it on October 10 and wrote in his diary that it was “very effective and left me greatly depressed.”

sources.title: entertainment‘The Day After’ 40th anniversary: How the ABC movie helped ...
'The Day After': This 1980s TV movie helped change the course of ...
The Day After - Wikipedia

the-day-after-1983.detail: Reagan's White House had feared this film would shake public resolve and reportedly asked ABC’s chairman to bury it. It was screened for the Joint Chiefs of Staff, Reagan’s rhetoric softened, and in 1987, as he and Mikhail Gorbachev signed their Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty, Soviet television broadcast it uncut.

time-machine-of-year-1983.summary: In January 1983 Time put a computer on its cover as Machine of the Year in place of a person. Since 1927 Time had chosen whoever had, “for better or for worse,” most influenced that year's events; this was its first inanimate choice, and only Endangered Earth, Planet of the Year for 1988, has followed. Its feature highlighted Steve Jobs, John Opel, Adam Osborne, Dan Bricklin, Jack Tramiel and Clive Sinclair, marking personal computers’ arrival in American homes and offices.

sources.title: Time Person of the Year - Wikipedia
Time, cover, "The Computer, Machine of the Year", 3 January 1983
sources.author: Time
sources.confirms: The magazine's own archive of the 3 January 1983 cover naming the computer Machine of the Year.

sources.title: National Museum of American History, 'Time Magazine Machine of the Year: The Computer Moves In' (object record, 3 January 1983 issue)
sources.author: Smithsonian National Museum of American History
sources.venue: Smithsonian National Museum of American History collections
sources.confirms: The 3 January 1983 issue of Time named the computer Machine of the Year in place of its Man or Person of the Year, with a cover showing a microcomputer and George Segal sculptures.

video-game-crash-1983.summary: In 1983 American video game sales began a fall from $3.2 billion to $100 million in two years. Atari’s VCS had dominated since its Space Invaders port in 1980, and after Activision opened third-party publishing in 1979, scores of inexperienced firms, about 100 by 1983, flooded stores with poor games; manufacturers raised output 175 percent against demand up 100 percent, while cheap home computers lured players away. Atari lost over $536 million in 1983, and the console market revived only when Nintendo’s NES arrived in October 1985.

sources.title: Video game crash of 1983 - Wikipedia
Video Games Industry Comes Down to Earth
sources.author: Kleinfield, N. R.
sources.confirms: By late 1983 the American video game industry was in a steep sales collapse after years of growth.

sources.author: Smithsonian National Museum of American History
sources.confirms: Atari buried unsold cartridges in a New Mexico landfill in 1983 as the market collapsed.

video-game-crash-1983.detail: Atari’s burial of unsold stock, including E.T. cartridges, in a landfill near Alamogordo, New Mexico, became this crash’s iconic image. When historians excavated it in 2014, former Atari executive James Heller said about 728,000 cartridges were buried, not the millions of legend.

wargames-1983.summary: In June 1983 WarGames showed a teenager dialling into NORAD and nearly starting a war; Reagan saw it and ordered a security review. Matthew Broderick plays David Lightman, a teenager who dials every number in Sunnyvale hunting for a game company and instead reaches WOPR, a NORAD supercomputer; when he picks “Global Thermonuclear War,” the machine plays in earnest. It grossed $125 million on a $12 million budget and earned three Oscar nominations, and President Ronald Reagan’s questions about its premise led to NSDD-145, America’s first computer security directive.

sources.title: WarGames
WarGames - AFI Catalog - American Film Institute
Kaplan, Fred, "'WarGames' and Cybersecurity's Debt to a Hollywood Hack", New York Times, 19 February 2016
sources.author: Kaplan, Fred
sources.confirms: Independent report that President Reagan watched the 1983 film and asked his advisers whether such an intrusion was possible, leading to the 1984 national security directive on computer security.

wargames-1983.detail:
After the 414s breached systems at Los Alamos National Laboratory later in 1983, news media called it the “WarGames” case and raised concerns about its scenario. Reagan, Lasker’s family friend, watched WarGames and ordered a national security review; within a week, his Joint Chiefs of Staff said its premise was technically possible, General John Vessey telling him “the problem is much worse than you think.”

Reagan’s interest led to NSDD-145, issued 18 months later, and WarGames also led to 1986’s Computer Fraud and Abuse Act.

aaai-winter-warning-1984.summary: In 1984 Roger Schank and Drew McDermott warned an AI conference that overpromising would bring an AI winter; it came within three years. Both had lived through AI’s funding drought of the 1970s. They warned business leaders that enthusiasm for AI had spiraled out of control and disappointment would follow, describing a chain reaction modelled on nuclear winter: pessimism inside AI, then in newspapers, then severe funding cuts, then serious research ending.

sources.qualifies: Minsky is not among the participants; the record's summary should name Schank and McDermott.

aaai-winter-warning-1984.verification_note: AI Magazine's record of the AAAI-84 panel 'The Dark Ages of AI' lists Drew McDermott, Mitchell Waldrop, B. Chandrasekaran, John McDermott and Roger Schank as participants; Marvin Minsky was not on the panel, so this warning came from Schank and McDermott.
aaai-winter-warning-1984.detail: Lisp machine makers collapsed in 1987 and DARPA cut its Strategic Computing AI budget, as they had predicted. The panel’s published record, “The Dark Ages of AI: A Panel Discussion at AAAI-84,” names Drew McDermott, M. Mitchell Waldrop, B. Chandrasekaran, John McDermott and Roger Schank as its panelists. AI’s earlier drought had followed Britain’s 1973 Lighthill report.

alvey-programme-1983.summary: In 1983 Britain launched the Alvey Programme, £350 million for information technology research, to answer Japan's Fifth Generation. Japan had invited Britain to join its project, and in October 1981 a Department of Industry mission of academics, civil servants and business representatives went to Tokyo to explore collaboration. Instead, a committee chaired by British Telecom technology director John Alvey proposed a different course of action: a government-sponsored programme funding British research in four areas, advanced microelectronics and VLSI chips, intelligent knowledge-based systems or AI, software engineering, and man-machine interaction including natural language processing.

sources.title: Alvey
'Alvey: Britain's Strategic Computing Initiative', ITNOW 32, no. 9 (1990), p. 26
sources.author: ITNOW (British Computer Society)
sources.confirms: Japan's 1981 Fifth Generation announcement prompted a committee under John Alvey whose proposals led to the five-year programme of 1983 to 1988 bearing his name.

sources.title: 'Expert Systems in the UK', IEEE Expert 5 (1990)
sources.author: IEEE Expert
sources.confirms: The Alvey Project was a five-year research and development programme for information technology begun in response to Japan's Fifth Generation initiative.

alvey-programme-1983.detail: Alvey’s programme supported knowledge engineering research across Britain rather than any single technology such as robotics; systems architecture, parallel processing in particular, featured in its VLSI work. Alvey was not involved in running it. Its operations have been likened to America’s DARPA and Japan’s ICOT.

apple-1984-ad.summary: In January 1984 Apple's Super Bowl ad showed a runner smashing Big Brother's screen; the Macintosh was sold as freedom from IBM. Rows of expressionless figures in grey suits watch a Big Brother-like face spout propaganda until an athlete in red shorts hurls a sledgehammer into his screen; its closing line promised that “1984 won’t be like 1984.” Apple intended its ad to introduce the Macintosh, which Apple announced two days later. It showed no product and named no price, yet it captured America’s attention and turned Super Bowl commercials into events in their own right.

The Apple '1984' Ad Changed the Super Bowl Forever
'Saying it With Pictures', Computer History Museum (1984)
sources.confirms: The page says Apple's 1984 Super Bowl commercial introduced the Macintosh and invited viewers to reject conformity and explore a new way of computing.

apple-1984-ad.detail: Agency Chiat/Day produced it for an estimated $400,000. Inside Apple it was controversial: some executives thought it too dark, too abstract and too expensive. Its legacy, by Britannica’s account, is Super Bowl advertising with teasers, celebrity cameos and seven-figure budgets, and a model for selling by telling a story rather than listing features.

att-breakup-1984.summary: On 1 January 1984 the Bell System split into AT&T and seven regional companies; long-distance prices fell and new networks got in. Until then its Bell System had run nearly all American telephone service, local and long distance, and made its equipment through Western Electric; America’s Justice Department had sued under antitrust law in 1974, and AT&T settled in 1982 by agreeing to give up local service while keeping long distance, Western Electric and Bell Labs. Seven independent companies formed from Bell System’s original twenty-two AT&T-controlled members, and AT&T’s book value fell by approximately 70%.

Brenner, Daniel L., "Divestiture of the Bell System", in Law and Regulation of Common Carriers in the Communications Industry (Routledge, 2018), pp. 159-167
sources.author: Brenner, Daniel L.

att-breakup-1984.detail: Competitors such as Sprint and MCI surged into long distance. AT&T’s gambit in exchange for divestiture, AT&T Computer Systems, failed. Western Electric was later spun off as Lucent. Among its offspring, Bell Atlantic acquired GTE in 2000 and became Verizon, and in 2005 SBC acquired its former parent and took AT&T’s name.

bataan-nuclear-plant-1984.summary: Westinghouse built a 620-megawatt pressurised water reactor at Napot Point in Morong, Bataan, under a contract signed by Ferdinand Marcos in 1976 and finished construction in 1984 at a cost near US$2.3 billion. Safety reviews flagged its site on a peninsula with Natib volcano and earthquake faults nearby, and Chernobyl's accident in April 1986 followed Marcos's fall by weeks; Corazon Aquino's government mothballed completed plant that year. Philippines paid off plant debt until 2007 while generating no power from it. A 2009 hazard study models tephra and lahar risks for site, and proposals to revive or convert plant recur.

bataan-nuclear-plant-1984.detail: A 2016 policy analysis treats Bataan as a case of sunk costs, corruption allegations around Westinghouse commissions and energy policy under martial law. Site now hosts tours. Record year marks construction completion; mothballing decision dates to 1986.

bhopal-disaster-1984.summary: In December 1984 a gas leak from a Union Carbide plant in Bhopal killed thousands overnight, the worst industrial accident ever. It took 45 to 60 minutes. Water had entered one of three 68,000-litre tanks and set off a runaway reaction while its flare tower was down for repairs and its gas scrubber stood on standby. Blown southeast over nearby communities, it exposed over 500,000 residents. Officials counted 2,259 immediate deaths, Madhya Pradesh later confirmed 3,787, and it remains history’s worst industrial disaster.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Bhopal disaster
E. Broughton, 'The Bhopal disaster and its aftermath: a review', Environmental Health 4 (2005), 6
sources.author: Edward Broughton
sources.confirms: On 3 December 1984 more than 40 tons of methyl isocyanate leaked at Bhopal, killing at least 3,800 people at once, with estimates of up to 10,000 deaths in the first days.

sources.confirms: Peer-reviewed review of the 1984 methyl isocyanate leak at Bhopal and its high initial mortality and lasting health effects.

bhopal-disaster-1984.detail:
Others estimate 8,000 or more died from gas-related diseases. Escaped gas rose to 40 tonnes within two hours. A 2006 government affidavit counted 558,125 injuries, including 38,478 temporary partial injuries and 3,900 severe and permanently disabling ones. Union Carbide, now owned by Dow Chemical, maintains that sabotage by an employee caused it.

In 1989 Union Carbide Corporation paid $470 million to settle litigation. It sold its 50.9% interest in its Indian subsidiary, a sale finalised in November 1994, and Dow Chemical purchased Union Carbide in 2001.

picture.credit: Martin Stott, Bhopal Medical Appeal, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

brazil-informatics-law-1984.summary: In 1984 Brazil banned imports of small computers to grow its own makers; prices rose, the industry lagged, and the law ended in 1992. Since the early 1970s Brazil’s military governments had reserved its computer market to domestic-capital firms to grow a national industry. The law authorizes transitional restrictions to protect national companies and assigns SEI, its informatics secretariat, duties that include reviewing projects and commenting on imports. Its market reserve built firms employing about 70,000 people by 1989, drew criticism for obsolete equipment and exorbitant prices, and ended in October 1992.

"Brazil: Informatics Law Concerning Policy of Market Reserve, Technology Transfer and Foreign Involvement", International Legal Materials 25, no. 4 (1986), pp. 868-883
sources.author: International Legal Materials (American Society of International Law)

brazil-informatics-law-1984.detail: Its reserve shut out IBM, Burroughs, HP and Olivetti. Critics also pointed to smuggling of foreign machines. SEI was run by colonels linked to SNI, Brazil’s military intelligence service. On 13 November 1987 President Ronald Reagan imposed sanctions on Brazilian goods, citing $105 million in harm to American firms. A new informatics law in 1991 set its reserve’s end.

cisco-founded-1984.summary: In December 1984 two Stanford staff, a married couple who ran computer facilities for Stanford’s computer science department and business school, founded Cisco to sell the router that joined Stanford's campus networks. They pioneered using a multiprotocol router, a box passing traffic between networks that speak different protocols, to connect distant computers over a local area network. Cisco went public in 1990, and by 2000 its market capitalization of $500 billion surpassed Microsoft’s as the world’s most valuable company, before it lost 80 percent of its value by 2002.

sources.title: Cisco - Wikipedia
Cisco, 'Cisco Celebrates 25 Years of Technology Innovation and Corporate Social Responsibility', newsroom release, December 2009
sources.author: Cisco Systems
sources.confirms: Cisco was founded on 10 December 1984 by former Stanford computer scientists Len Bosack and Sandy Lerner, whose work on linking campus networks produced the first multiprotocol router.

sources.title: 'Cisco Systems', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: Cisco was founded in December 1984 by Leonard Bosack and Sandra Lerner, who ran computer facilities for two Stanford departments and linked their networks using technology devised by other Stanford staff.

cisco-founded-1984.detail:
Cisco’s software descended from Stanford’s “Blue Box” router, which used circuitry by Andy Bechtolsheim and software written by research engineer William Yeager. Bosack and Stanford employee Kirk Lougheed adapted it into what became Cisco IOS. On July 11, 1986, both were forced to resign from Stanford, which weighed criminal complaints before licensing its router software and two boards to Cisco in 1987.

Bill Graves served as first CEO from 1987 to 1988, followed by John Morgridge. Cisco’s name comes from San Francisco, and its logo depicts Golden Gate Bridge’s towers.

computer-virus-cohen-1984.summary: In 1984 Fred Cohen's paper named the computer virus and showed one taking over a Unix system in minutes. Such a program, when run, writes copies of its own code into other programs, which infect further programs in turn. Self-replicating code already existed: Creeper had spread across ARPANET in 1971, and Elk Cloner had infected Apple II floppies in 1982. In 1987 Cohen showed no algorithm can detect all viruses, and that year (c)Brain, first IBM PC virus in the wild, spread from Lahore, Pakistan.

sources.title: Computer virus (Wikipedia)
Cohen, Fred, 'Computer Viruses: Theory and Experiments', Computers and Security 6, no. 1 (1987), 22-35
sources.author: Cohen, Fred
sources.confirms: Cohen's paper introduces computer viruses, shows that viral defence is infeasible in large classes of systems, and reports his experiments; the ACM record cites the 1984 conference version.

sources.title: Stoll, Clifford, 'An Epidemiology of Viruses and Network Worms', and other papers citing Cohen, 'Computer Viruses', Proceedings of the 7th DoD/NBS Computer Security Conference (1984)
sources.author: ACM SIGSAC Review
sources.confirms: Contemporary ACM papers cite Cohen's 'Computer Viruses' in the Proceedings of the 7th DoD/NBS Computer Security Conference, 1984, fixing the 1984 date.

computer-virus-cohen-1984.detail: Bob Thomas wrote Creeper at BBN Technologies in 1971; it infected DEC PDP-10 computers over ARPANET; Reaper was written to delete it. Richard Skrenta wrote Elk Cloner in 1981 as a ninth grader near Pittsburgh; it was the first personal computer virus to appear outside its author’s lab. Amjad Farooq Alvi and Basit Farooq Alvi created (c)Brain in 1986, reportedly to deter unauthorized copying of software they had written. Cohen’s own theoretical compression virus showed that a virus need not be malware.

cyc-1984.summary: In late 1984 Douglas Lenat began Cyc, an attempt to type in all of common sense by hand; thirty years and millions of rules later it was being commercialised. His project aimed to assemble a comprehensive ontology and knowledge base of common-sense knowledge about how the world works, facts so obvious that people never write them down and machines never learn them. Its method was hand-written axioms in its own logical language, CycL, read by an inference engine. Cyc’s knowledge base grew from about 1 million assertions in 1994 to about 24.5 million by 2017, consuming $60 million and 600 person-years by 2002.

sources.author: Knight, Will

cyc-1984.verification_note: A 2016 source dates the start to late 1984 rather than July and counts 31 years of work, describing Cyc as being commercialised.
cyc-1984.detail: Its programmers, philosophers and other contributors are known as Cyclists. Cyc’s name comes from “encyclopedia” and is a registered trademark of Cycorp, which took over its development. CycL has a published specification and dozens of heuristic-level modules appear in Lenat and Guha’s textbook, but Cyc’s inference engine code remains Cycorp property. In 2008 Cyc resources were mapped to many Wikipedia articles.

dynatac-8000x-1984.summary: In 1984 the DynaTAC 8000X reached customers at $3,995; the mobile phone became a product, if only for the rich. It was the first commercially available handheld cellular phone and was priced at US$3,995 in 1984. Motorola had announced Dyna-Tac, short for Dynamic Adaptive Total Area Coverage, in April 1973 after John F. Mitchell’s team, Martin Cooper among them, built portable cellular telephony. Its LED display dialed or recalled one of 30 numbers, and one charge gave about 30 minutes of talk. Its much smaller successor MicroTAC replaced it from 1989.

dynatac-8000x-1984.detail: Its first prototype call reportedly reached a wrong number. Motorola had petitioned America’s FCC for cellular channels since 1947. Mitchell was among Motorola employees granted a patent for portable cellular work in 1973. Its retail price of $3,995 equals roughly $12,400 in 2025 dollars. Models followed from 1985’s 8000s to 1993’s Classic II; by StarTAC’s release in 1996 DynaTAC was obsolete.

frozen-embryo-birth-monash-1984.summary: Alan Trounson and Linda Mohr of Monash University reported a pregnancy from a cryopreserved eight-cell embryo in Nature in 1983, though it miscarried. On 28 March 1984 a healthy girl was delivered by caesarean section at Queen Victoria Medical Centre to a couple treated by Carl Wood's team; news was released on 10 April. Embryos had been frozen in a controlled-rate freezer for two months before transfer. Trounson and Wood's 1984 review summarises Monash results from 1979 to 1982. Embryo freezing allowed spare embryos from stimulated cycles to be stored, reducing repeat egg collection, and most IVF transfers worldwide now use frozen embryos. It also provoked Victoria's Infertility (Medical Procedures) Act 1984.

indonesia-rice-self-sufficiency-1984.summary: Indonesia imported more rice than any other country in 1960s. Through BIMAS mass guidance programmes, subsidised fertiliser and pesticide, irrigation repair, IRRI-derived varieties and floor prices run by logistics agency BULOG, average yields rose from about 2 to 4.5 tonnes per hectare between 1970s and 1980s, and in 1984 harvest met domestic demand without imports. Suharto addressed FAO's fortieth-anniversary conference in Rome in 1985 and received its medal for this result. Brown planthopper outbreaks fed by pesticide overuse soon followed, prompting a 1986 decree that banned 57 insecticides and backed integrated pest management, and imports resumed in 1990s.

indonesia-rice-self-sufficiency-1984.detail: Leon Mears' 1984 survey in Bulletin of Indonesian Economic Studies analyses policy mix; Thorburn's 2015 review in Insects records yield figures and pest crisis. Self-sufficiency lasted only a few years, and later governments revived it as a political goal.

information-wants-to-be-free-1984.summary: In 1984 Stewart Brand told hackers at their first conference that information wants to be free, because distribution's cost keeps falling. He said information “wants to be expensive, because it's so valuable,” then: “On the other hand, information wants to be free, because the cost of getting it out is getting lower and lower all the time. So you have these two fighting against each other.” Only its second half survived, as a slogan in decades of fights over copyright and open information.

Wozniak replied: “Information should be free but your time should not.” Brand later told Levy his remark was off the cuff, riffing on Levy’s own line “Information Should Be Free.”

itaipu-dam-1984.summary: In 1984 Itaipu's first turbine spun on the Brazil-Paraguay border; it became Earth's largest power plant until Three Gorges. Brazil and Paraguay had built it together on their Paraná River border, 15 km north of their Friendship Bridge, under a 1973 treaty, with construction from 1975 and its dam completed in 1982; its reservoir displaced 10,000 families and drowned Guaíra Falls, among the world’s largest waterfalls. Water falling 118 metres turns 20 units of 700 MW each, 14 GW in all, installed over two decades. Only China’s Three Gorges produces more hydroelectricity, and Itaipu’s 103.1 TWh in 2016 stood as a world record until 2020.

itaipu-dam-1984.detail: Itaipu holds the world’s 45th largest reservoir. Three Gorges, with 22,500 MW capacity, beat its record with 111.8 TWh in 2020 after heavy monsoon rain. From 2012 to 2021 Itaipu averaged 89.22 TWh a year, second to Three Gorges at 97.22 TWh.

koeberg-nuclear-1984.summary: In 1984 Koeberg near Cape Town joined the grid, still Africa's only nuclear power station. Unit 1 was synchronized on 4 April 1984, and Unit 2 followed on 25 July 1985. Eskom, South Africa’s state-owned utility, owns and operates its two pressurised water reactors, built to a Framatome design from France. Commissioning had been delayed by nearly 18 months after Rodney Wilkinson, acting for the African National Congress’s armed wing Umkhonto we Sizwe, planted bombs inside it during construction, causing about $519 million in damage.
