koeberg-nuclear-1984.detail: South Africa’s 2019 Integrated Resource Plan allows Koeberg to run through 2044. Wilkinson had served in South Africa’s defence force and worked at Koeberg during construction, smuggling in plans and then explosives. In September 2020 Eskom announced it would replace Koeberg’s six steam generators under a ZAR 4.4 billion ($240 million) contract with Areva.

macintosh-1984.summary: In January 1984 Apple's Macintosh brought the mouse and windows to the mass market; computing stopped meaning typed commands. It went on sale two days later, on January 24, at US$2,495, bundled with MacWrite and MacPaint. Its motherboard, 9-inch monochrome screen and floppy drive sat in a beige case with a carrying handle, driven by keyboard and single-button mouse, so buyers could write and draw by pointing and clicking. It was history’s first successful mass-market all-in-one desktop computer with graphical interface.

macintosh-1984.detail: Sales reached 70,000 units by May 3, 1984. Jef Raskin began Macintosh in 1979, while Lisa was becoming a GUI machine, as a low-cost, easy-to-use computer with text-based interface. Steve Jobs later remade it around Lisa’s graphical approach. Its design helped establish desktop publishing as a general office function. On its successor Macintosh 512K’s release, it was rebranded Macintosh 128K.

neuromancer-1984.summary: In 1984 William Gibson's Neuromancer coined cyberspace and imagined hackers and rogue AIs years before the public web. His debut follows Case, a washed-up hacker barred from cyberspace, hired by shadowy ex-officer Armitage and razorgirl Molly for a job that serves Wintermute, an artificial intelligence with purposes of its own. Gibson had feared, after seeing 1982’s Blade Runner, that readers would think he had copied its “fine visual texture.” Neuromancer became a foundational work of early cyberpunk and remains history’s only novel to win Hugo, Nebula and Philip K. Dick awards.

sources.confirms: Gibson's debut novel Neuromancer popularized the concept of cyberspace and won the Nebula, Hugo and Philip K. Dick awards.

neuromancer-1984.detail: Armitage cures Case, then holds him with a time-delayed poison until his job is done. Wintermute found Corto, a broken ex-soldier, and built its Armitage personality over him to direct its team; in Istanbul they recruit Peter Riviera, psychopathic police spy and holographic illusionist. Gibson wrote in his introduction to Neuromancer’s graphic novel that Blade Runner was not a conscious influence. In 2005 Time named Neuromancer among its All-Time 100 Novels; its success raised Gibson from relative obscurity.

newspapers-peak-1984.summary: In 1984 American newspapers sold 63 million copies a day, their peak; by 2022 they sold a third of that. By 2022 it was about 20.9 million, a third of that peak, as readers moved first to cable news and then to websites and phones.

ok-tedi-mine-tailings-1984.summary: BHP-led Ok Tedi Mining began producing gold in 1984 from Mount Fubilan in Papua New Guinea's Star Mountains. In January 1984 a landslide destroyed foundations of its half-built tailings dam at Ok Ma; with government approval, company began releasing tailings and waste rock directly into Ok Tedi and Fly River, eventually about 80,000 tonnes a day. Field measurements found copper-rich sediment spreading along 1,000 kilometres of river, raising riverbeds, killing forest across thousands of hectares and destroying fisheries for 50,000 downstream people. Yonggom and other landowners sued BHP in Melbourne in 1994, winning a 1996 settlement, but discharge continued. BHP exited in 2002, calling mine incompatible with its environmental values.

ok-tedi-mine-tailings-1984.detail: Campaigning and litigation ran for two decades. Company consultants described interim tailings arrangements, approved after dam collapse, in 1986. A 1989 cyanide spill compounded damage. Ok Tedi funded a large share of PNG's export income and government budget, which shaped decisions to keep operating. Mine, now state-owned, continues to discharge under agreements with affected communities, with dieback zone exceeding 1,500 square kilometres.

project-sida-kinshasa-1984.summary: In October 1983 a Belgian, American and Zairean team spent three weeks at Mama Yemo Hospital in Kinshasa and found 38 patients with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome, women and men in near equal numbers, with no link to homosexuality, transfusion or drugs. Their Lancet paper of July 1984 estimated at least 17 cases per 100,000 and argued for heterosexual transmission, reshaping understanding of a disease then framed around gay men in American cities. Projet SIDA, set up in Kinshasa in 1984 under Jonathan Mann with Zairean clinicians, became a leading research site on African AIDS until it collapsed in 1991 unrest.

sources.author: Piot, Peter; Quinn, Thomas C.; Taelman, Henri; et al.
sources.confirms: 38 patients in 3 weeks of 1983 at Mama Yemo Hospital; male to female ratio 1.1:1; at least 17 per 100,000; heterosexual transmission

sources.author: International Commission

project-sida-kinshasa-1984.detail: Co-authors included Bila Kapita and other Kinshasa physicians; Peter Piot later led UNAIDS. Serological work on Zairean samples from the 1970s showed HIV had circulated in Kinshasa for decades. Projet SIDA's studies documented mother-to-child transmission, prevalence among blood donors and health workers, and heterosexual spread in Kinshasa, with findings published through 1980s. Its Zairean leadership under Bila Kapita and Nzila Nzilambi trained a generation of African HIV researchers.

san-juanico-lpg-explosion-1984.summary: At about 05:35 on 19 November 1984 a pipe ruptured during filling at PEMEX's liquefied petroleum gas terminal in San Juan Ixhuatepec, Tlalnepantla. A vapour cloud roughly 200 by 150 metres drifted to a ground flare and ignited; within fifteen minutes storage spheres and cylinders began failing in boiling-liquid expanding-vapour explosions, hurling fragments up to a kilometre into a dense neighbourhood that had grown around the plant. Around 500 people died, several thousand were burned, and some 60,000 were evacuated. Investigations faulted a gas-detection system that did not isolate supply, layout and separation distances, and absence of land-use control. Alongside Bhopal two weeks later, San Juanico reshaped process-safety rules and burn care planning.

sources.title: Pietersen, C. M., 'Analysis of the LPG-disaster in Mexico City', Journal of Hazardous Materials 20 (1988)
sources.author: Pietersen, C. M.
sources.confirms: Sequence of release, ignition and BLEVEs; casualty estimate of 650 dead and 6,500 injured.
sources.qualifies: Casualty figures higher than HSE and Arturson.

sources.confirms: 05:35 pipe rupture; cloud 200 by 150 by 2 metres; first BLEVE about 15 minutes later; some 500 killed; failures in isolation and layout.

sources.author: Arturson, G.
sources.confirms: Medical response, about 500 dead and 7,000 injured, burn-care lessons.

san-juanico-lpg-explosion-1984.verification_note: Death toll differs: HSE and Arturson give about 500; Pietersen gives 650 dead and 6,500 injured. Summary uses the lower, more widely repeated figure.
san-juanico-lpg-explosion-1984.detail: Pietersen's hazard analysis in Journal of Hazardous Materials counts 650 dead and 6,500 injured; UK HSE's case study and Arturson's Burns paper give around 500 dead and about 7,000 injured. Exact counts remain contested. The terminal held six spheres and 48 cylinders with about 11,000 cubic metres of LPG, operated by PEMEX since 1962, and distributed gas to much of Mexico City. Houses had been built within 130 metres of tanks. Fifteen BLEVEs occurred over ninety minutes; one fragment of a sphere weighing tens of tonnes travelled 1,200 metres. Films of fireballs became teaching material for emergency planners.

terminator-1984.summary: In 1984 The Terminator gave the public its image of AI turned hostile, Skynet, a reference every AI debate still reaches for. In its plot, Skynet, a hostile artificial intelligence system, sends a cyborg assassin, played by Arnold Schwarzenegger, back from post-apocalyptic 2029 to 1984 Los Angeles to kill Sarah Connor (Linda Hamilton), whose future son will save humanity, while soldier Kyle Reese (Michael Biehn) travels back to protect her. Defying low expectations, it topped America’s box office for two weeks and grossed $78.3 million against a $6.4 million budget, launching Cameron’s career and a franchise.

terminator-1984.detail: Its success confirmed Schwarzenegger as leading man and spawned sequels, a television series, comics and games. Cameron devised its premise from a fever dream during his first film Piranha II’s release in 1982 and developed it with William Wisher Jr. He sold its rights to Gale Anne Hurd on condition that he direct; Hurd secured Orion Pictures as distributor, and Hemdale’s John Daly and Derek Gibson arranged financing. Orion first approached Schwarzenegger for Reese; he took the title role after befriending Cameron. In 2008 America’s Library of Congress selected The Terminator for America’s National Film Registry.

tetris-1984.summary: In 1984 Alexey Pajitnov wrote Tetris on a Soviet computer in Moscow; the falling blocks became the most ported game in history. He wrote it on an Elektronika 60, a Soviet clone of DEC’s PDP-11, after buying a pentomino puzzle set and cutting its twelve five-square shapes to seven four-square tetrominoes; players rotate and place falling pieces, and any completed line vanishes. Free floppy copies spread through Moscow and Eastern Europe, and with 520 million copies sold by 2022 Tetris ranks as history’s best-selling video game.

sources.title: Tetris (Wikipedia)
Tetris game cartridge
sources.author: Computer History Museum
sources.confirms: Alexey Pajitnov designed Tetris on an Electronica 60 while working for the Soviet Academy of Sciences in Moscow in 1984.

sources.title: Hadjimatheou, Chloe. 'How Tetris Became the World's Favourite Computer Game.' BBC News, 30 December 2011.
sources.author: Chloe Hadjimatheou
sources.confirms: Confirms Pajitnov wrote Tetris in 1984 at the Moscow Academy of Sciences computing centre, inspired by pentominoes, and that it spread by copied disks.

sources.author: Julien Mailland

tetris-1984.detail:
Its name joins “tetra” with his favourite sport, tennis; Pajitnov had judged twelve pentomino shapes too complicated. He wrote it in Pascal for RT-11 in about three weeks. His machine had no graphics, so brackets and spaces stood in for blocks, and his first version had no scoring or levels. Colleagues ported it to the IBM PC.

Robert Stein of Andromeda Software saw Tetris in Hungary and sublicensed it to Mirrorsoft in Britain and Spectrum HoloByte in America; Nintendo released Game Boy and NES versions in 1989, and its Game Boy version sold over 35 million. After Nintendo’s license expired in 1995, Pajitnov claimed his rights and founded The Tetris Company with Henk Rogers. Tetris entered the World Video Game Hall of Fame’s inaugural class in 2015.

wargames-nsdd-145-1984.summary: In 1984 Reagan, shaken by the film WarGames, signed the first national policy on computer security. General John Vessey, chairman of the Joint Chiefs, returned a week later: “Mr. President, the problem is much worse than you think.” Fifteen months of interagency memos, working groups and studies followed, and Reagan signed NSDD-145, titled “National Policy on Telecommunications and Automated Information Systems Security,” on September 17, 1984. It warned that government’s new computers were “highly susceptible to interception, unauthorized electronic access and related forms of technical exploitation” and gave NSA a lead role in securing them.

wargames-nsdd-145-1984.detail: Vessey’s answer came from Don Latham, formerly of NSA and then assistant secretary of defense for command, control, communications and intelligence. Had Latham’s language stood, security standards for every computer in America, government, business and personal, would have fallen under NSA’s gaze, which Congress resisted. Anti-hacking bills followed in a comprehensive crime bill, with WarGames clips screened at committee hearings.

arabsat-1a-1985.summary: In February 1985 Arabsat-1A reached orbit, the first satellite owned by the Arab states together. Arab information ministers had set out principles for a shared satellite network in 1967, and on 14 April 1976 Arabsat was formed under Arab League jurisdiction to serve its member states’ information, cultural and educational needs, with Saudi Arabia its main financier and Riyadh its headquarters. Its satellites sit in geostationary orbit over 21 member countries. Shortly after launch Arabsat-1A’s solar panel failed to extend properly; after other faults it was relegated to backup behind Arabsat-1B.

sources.venue: NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive

sources.author: Mohammad K. Samarkandy
sources.venue: IEEE International Symposium on Electromagnetic Compatibility
sources.confirms: 1985 IEEE paper describing the Arabsat system shared by the Arab states; Crossref metadata confirmed.

arabsat-1a-1985.detail: Arabsat-1B was deployed from Space Shuttle Discovery in June 1985 and carried its service. Arabsat-1A was abandoned in late 1991 and switched off in 1992; Arabsat-1B followed in 1993. Each satellite reached geosynchronous orbit by firing its own hydrazine and nitrogen tetroxide motor, keeping remaining propellant for station-keeping. Arabsat has launched satellites from 1985 through 2019, and all Arab League states except Comoros hold shares, Saudi Arabia 36.7% and Kuwait 14.6% among them.

arm-1985.summary: In April 1985 the first ARM processor worked on its first try at Acorn in Cambridge; its descendants dominate smartphones, with over 230 billion ARM chips produced by 2022. Sophie Wilson and Steve Furber, who had built Acorn’s BBC Micro around a 6502, wanted more processing speed than any chip maker then sold, and after visiting Berkeley’s RISC project designed their own reduced instruction set chip with VLSI Technology making the silicon. ARM1 had about 25,000 transistors, against 134,000 in Intel’s 80286. Its successor ARM2 powered Acorn’s Archimedes in 1987, and in 1990 Acorn, Apple and VLSI spun out Advanced RISC Machines.

arm-1985.detail: Furber and Wilson had earlier adopted Acorn’s Tube coprocessor interface and found low-cost, high-performance designs possible after Western Design Center showed them its 6502 successor work. Its reduced instruction set kept it small and cool, and ARM1 served first as a second processor for the BBC Micro. Advanced RISC Machines was formed to supply Apple’s Newton and adopted a licensing model that put ARM cores in other companies’ chips; by 2022 over 230 billion ARM chips had been produced, making it the most widely used instruction set architecture, dominant in smartphones.

bayesian-networks-1985.summary: In 1985 Judea Pearl named Bayesian networks, diagrams that let computers reason under uncertainty. He meant it to emphasize three aspects: subjective input information, reliance on Bayes’s conditioning as its basis for updating information, and a distinction between causal and evidential modes of reasoning. Such a network represents variables as nodes in a directed acyclic graph, arrows marking conditional dependencies, so a model can compute how likely one event is given evidence about others. Pearl’s 1988 book Probabilistic Reasoning in Intelligent Systems brought probability back into AI, and he received 2011’s Turing Award.

sources.confirms: Pearl's 1985 paper introduces Bayesian networks as directed acyclic graphs whose nodes are propositions and whose arcs carry conditional probabilities, with belief propagated locally between nodes.

sources.confirms: The term Bayesian network was coined by Pearl in 1985 to stress the subjective nature of the input information, reliance on Bayes conditioning, and the distinction between causal and evidential reasoning.

bayesian-networks-1985.detail: Pearl named his networks after Thomas Bayes, author of Bayes’s rule. Richard Neapolitan’s 1989 text Probabilistic Reasoning in Expert Systems summarized their properties, and together with Pearl’s book established Bayesian networks as a research field in late 1980s AI.

boltzmann-machine-1985.summary: In 1985 David Ackley, Geoffrey Hinton and Terrence Sejnowski published the Boltzmann machine, a network that learns using random noise. A Boltzmann machine is a network of stochastic binary units whose joint behavior is governed by an energy function modelled on a spin glass from statistical physics; hidden units let it learn internal representations, and its learning rule compares unit correlations with data clamped against those in free running. Hinton later said he devised its algorithm in early 1983 for a talk on simulated annealing in Hopfield networks.

sources.confirms: Peer-reviewed encyclopaedia article by the co-inventor describing the Boltzmann machine as a network of stochastic binary units with a learning rule derived from statistical mechanics, introduced in the 1985 paper with Ackley and Sejnowski.

boltzmann-machine-1985.detail: Its model is the Sherrington–Kirkpatrick spin glass, and that analogy gave neural network research vocabulary borrowed from physics, such as energy. Douglas Hofstadter’s 1984 Copycat project applied an Ising model with annealed Gibbs sampling at the same time. General Boltzmann machines proved impractical to train, but restricted Boltzmann machines, trained with Hinton’s contrastive divergence, formed deep belief networks in the 2000s and seeded deep learning; Hinton and John Hopfield shared 2024’s Nobel Prize in Physics for such work.

buckminsterfullerene-1985.summary: In 1985 chemists in Texas found a molecule of 60 carbon atoms shaped like a football. Smalley’s laser vaporized graphite into helium gas to form carbon clusters, and their mass spectrometer showed an outsized peak at 60 atoms; they deduced a closed cage of 12 pentagons and 20 hexagons and named it after Buckminster Fuller’s geodesic domes. Kroto, Curl and Smalley shared 1996’s Nobel Prize in Chemistry, and their fullerenes opened carbon nanotechnology, nanotubes and graphene among it.

buckminsterfullerene-1985.detail: Its shape is a truncated icosahedron, and their report appeared in Nature in 1985. Eiji Osawa had predicted C60 theoretically in 1970, and Rohlfing, Cox and Kaldor had detected 60-atom clusters in 1984 without identifying their structure. Kroto came to Rice hoping to simulate carbon chains in red giant stars. In 1990 Wolfgang Krätschmer and Donald Huffman produced C60 in bulk by arc discharge between graphite rods, making fullerene chemistry practical, and Sumio Iijima’s carbon nanotubes followed in 1991.

cable-half-1985.summary: By 1985 cable television reached 42.8 percent of American television households, up from under 8 percent in 1968, and passed half in 1988 to 1989; it would pass 65 percent before 2000.

fews-famine-early-warning-1985.summary: In 1985 USAID set up a famine early warning network after Ethiopia; satellites and price data now flag hunger months ahead. Famines in Sudan and Ethiopia in 1984 and 1985 had killed hundreds of thousands while governments learned of them too late. It combined satellite imagery of rainfall and vegetation from NASA, NOAA and USGS with USDA crop data, market prices and field reports to forecast food insecurity months ahead, so donors could ship aid before people starved. It covered over 30 countries and warned of Somalia’s 2011 famine before going dark in January 2025 when USAID was dismantled.

fews-famine-early-warning-1985.detail: Operated by contractor Chemonics, FEWS NET classified districts on the five-step Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) scale from minimal to famine. Its reports were public and used by UN agencies and aid groups as well as American officials. After its January 2025 shutdown left humanitarian agencies without its forecasts, parts of its work were restored later in 2025.

free-software-foundation-1985.summary: In October 1985 Richard Stallman founded the Free Software Foundation to support GNU; software you may study and change had an institution. He had announced GNU in September 1983 to build a Unix-like operating system anyone could use freely. FSF defines free software by four freedoms: to run a program, study and change it, share copies, and share changed versions. Its legal tool is copyleft: its GNU General Public License, first published in 1989, lets anyone copy and modify code but requires derived works to carry its same terms. GNU tools plus Linus Torvalds’s kernel became GNU/Linux.

sources.title: 'Free Software Foundation', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: Records that Richard Stallman founded the Free Software Foundation in 1985 to support the GNU project he had announced in 1983.

free-software-foundation-1985.detail: GNU/Linux runs much of today’s Internet. FSF employed programmers for GNU software in its early years and later shifted to legal and campaign work, including GPL enforcement and campaigns against digital restrictions management. Stallman served as president until resigning in 2019 amid controversy over his comments, and rejoined its board in 2021.

intel-386-1985.summary: In October 1985 Intel's 386 brought 32-bit computing to the PC. Its 275,000 transistors gave it 32-bit registers, a 4 GB address space, memory paging and a protected mode with virtual 8086 mode, so one machine could run several DOS programs safely at once. Compaq shipped its Deskpro 386 in June 1986, seven months before IBM used the chip, shifting leadership of PC design from IBM to clone makers. Its architecture underpinned Windows 3.x, Linux and a generation of software.

intel-386-1985.detail: Its first version ran at 16 MHz on a 1.5 µm process, and Intel kept producing it for embedded systems until September 2007. IBM, having invested heavily in its 80286-based PC/AT, waited until 1987’s PS/2 Model 80 to adopt it, and Compaq’s decision to build its own 386 machine ended IBM’s power to set PC standards. Linus Torvalds wrote his kernel for the 386 in 1991, and its instruction set, extended since, still runs most desktop software.

iran-health-houses-behvarz-1985.summary: Building on 1970s pilots in West Azerbaijan and Alma-Ata's 1978 primary care declaration, Iran's new Ministry of Health and Medical Education, created in 1985, extends a network of khaneh-ye behdasht, health houses, each serving about 1,500 people in a village and its satellites. Staff are behvarz, a man and a woman chosen from that community and trained for two years in vaccination, antenatal care, growth monitoring, family planning and recording every household in a vital horoscope ledger. By 2000 some 16,000 health houses cover more than 90 percent of rural Iran. Rural infant mortality falls from about 120 per 1,000 births in 1974 to under 30 by 2000, and urban-rural gaps narrow; Mississippi later copies this model in its Delta counties.

mexico-city-earthquake-1985.summary: At 07:17 on 19 September 1985 a magnitude 8.0 earthquake on the Cocos plate boundary off Michoacán sent waves across 350 kilometres to Mexico City, where soft clay of former Lake Texcoco resonated at periods near two seconds, amplifying ground motion severalfold and prolonging it. Buildings of six to fifteen storeys, tuned to similar periods, failed in Centro, Roma and Tlatelolco, including Hospital Juárez and Nuevo León tower; official death tolls ran from about 5,000 to more than 10,000, with hundreds of thousands displaced. Seismologists used dense records to explain site effects; engineers rewrote Mexico's building code in 1987 with zoning by soil, and citizens' rescue brigades fed a civil-society movement. An alert system warning of coastal quakes followed in 1991.

sources.title: Beck, Susan L.; Hall, Jonathan M., 'Factors contributing to the catastrophe in Mexico City during the earthquake of September 19, 1985', Geophysical Research Letters 13, no. 6 (1986)
sources.author: Beck, Susan L.; Hall, Jonathan M.

mexico-city-earthquake-1985.verification_note: Casualty totals vary widely between official (about 5,000 to 6,000) and civil-society estimates (10,000 or more); summary gives the range.
mexico-city-earthquake-1985.detail: Long duration and lake-sediment resonance account for damage patterns, and Emilio Rosenblueth's group set out seismic zoning adopted for Mexico City after 1985. Casualty figures remain disputed, from government's 6,000 to NGO estimates above 10,000. A magnitude 7.5 aftershock on 20 September toppled more weakened structures. Lack of government response in first days led neighbourhood groups and tenants' unions to organise rescue and housing demands, feeding 1988 electoral upheaval. Television's Televisa headquarters was damaged and its telephone exchange failure cut long-distance service, exposing fragile infrastructure.

narmada-bachao-sardar-sarovar-1985.summary: World Bank approves 450 million dollars in 1985 for Sardar Sarovar dam on Narmada, meant to irrigate Gujarat and generate 1,450 megawatts while submerging villages in three states. Medha Patkar and displaced Adivasi and farming communities form Narmada Bachao Andolan, holding fasts and long marches and refusing to move. Under pressure, Bank president Barber Conable commissions a review under Bradford Morse. Its report of 18 June 1992 finds resettlement and environmental work deficient and both India and Bank responsible. India asks Bank to withdraw in March 1993. Construction continues under Indian funding and a 2000 Supreme Court judgment, with height reaching 138.68 metres in 2017. Morse review leads to creation of Bank's Inspection Panel.

niger-farmer-regreening-1985.summary: From the mid-1980s, after drought years, farmers in Niger's Maradi and Zinder regions stopped clearing tree stumps and shoots from millet fields and began pruning and protecting them. Species such as Faidherbia albida returned in dense on-farm parklands. Satellite imagery and field surveys put regreening at about five million hectares, cutting wind erosion and adding fodder, firewood, fruit and crop yield. A 1980s shift in practice that let farmers claim trees they tended, rather than treating them as state property, helped the spread. Chris Reij calls it another kind of green revolution, achieved with little aid or government intervention.

sources.author: Reij, Chris; Tappan, Gray; Smale, Melinda
sources.confirms: Farmer-managed natural regeneration in southern Niger over an estimated five million hectares; reduced wind erosion; more crops, fodder, firewood, fruit; benefits to women; reduced migration

niger-farmer-regreening-1985.detail: Evidence set out in 2009 covers Niger and Burkina Faso; a 2014 chapter stresses that recovery occurred in densely populated areas without major projects. A 200 million tree figure appears in press accounts and in neither of these studies.

ozone-hole-discovery-1985.summary: In May 1985 British scientists reported a hole in ozone over Antarctica; within two years nations had agreed to ban its cause. Spring ozone over Halley Research Station had fallen by about a third since the 1970s. Mario Molina and Sherwood Rowland had predicted in 1974 that chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) from aerosols and refrigerants would release chlorine high in the stratosphere. On ice clouds above Antarctica that chlorine destroys ozone in a chain reaction as sunlight returns each spring. Their finding led to 1987’s Montreal Protocol, which phased out CFCs worldwide.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Ozone depletion

sources.author: Farman, J. C.; Gardiner, B. G.; Shanklin, J. D.

sources.author: Susan Solomon, Rolando R. Garcia, F. Sherwood Rowland and Donald J. Wuebbles
sources.confirms: Total ozone at Halley Bay in Antarctic spring (October) 1980 to 1984 was about 30 percent lower than in 1957 to 1973, and the paper proposes heterogeneous chlorine chemistry on polar stratospheric clouds as the cause.
sources.qualifies: The Montreal Protocol of 1987 scheduled phased cuts in CFC production rather than an immediate ban.

ozone-hole-discovery-1985.detail: Halley had measured ozone since 1957, and NASA’s Nimbus 7 satellite had recorded the same low values but its software had flagged them as errors. 1985's Vienna Convention set a framework, and Montreal Protocol followed in September 1987. Molina, Rowland and Paul Crutzen shared 1995’s Nobel Prize in Chemistry, and Antarctic ozone is projected to recover around 2066.

postman-amusing-ourselves-1985.summary: In 1985 Neil Postman argued that television turns every subject into entertainment; the argument was reapplied to every medium since. Its foreword argues that Aldous Huxley’s Brave New World, not George Orwell’s 1984, had come true: no one needed to ban books when no one wanted to read them. Postman, a New York University media theorist, held that each medium shapes what can be said in it; print America of the Lincoln–Douglas debates sustained hours of argument, while television reduces news, religion and politics to entertainment. His book sold about 200,000 copies and appeared in translation across more than a dozen languages.

Amusing Ourselves to Death: Public Discourse in the Age ...
Llorente, Renzo, 'Neil Postman', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.author: Llorente, Renzo
sources.confirms: Records that Amusing Ourselves to Death (1985), Postman's most influential work, argued that television reduces politics, news and history to entertainment and trivialises public discourse.

postman-amusing-ourselves-1985.verification_note: Sales near 200,000 copies are widely reported; translation counts differ between accounts (eight to sixteen languages).
postman-amusing-ourselves-1985.detail: Television’s “Now… this,” cutting from famine to a commercial, is Postman’s emblem of discourse without context. He developed his argument from a talk at 1984’s Frankfurt Book Fair, where he was asked to speak on Orwell’s year. Its 20th anniversary edition appeared in 2005 with a foreword by his son Andrew Postman, and Roger Waters’s 1992 album Amused to Death took its title from Postman’s book.

proton-saga-launch-1985.summary: Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad drives a Proton Saga off its Shah Alam line on 9 July 1985. Perusahaan Otomobil Nasional, formed in 1983 by state heavy industries corporation HICOM with Mitsubishi Motors and Mitsubishi Corporation, assembles a rebadged Mitsubishi Lancer Fiore with 1.3 and 1.5 litre engines. Tariff protection, excise exemptions and government fleet purchases give Proton most of Malaysia's passenger car market by 1990. Economists studying Malaysia's heavy industry drive note persistent reliance on Japanese components and low exports, and Proton's share fell after 2000 as Perodua and imports grew; Geely bought 49.9 percent in 2017.

rainbow-warrior-bombing-1985.summary: Just before midnight on 10 July 1985, two limpet mines planted by French DGSE agents sank Greenpeace's Rainbow Warrior at Marsden Wharf, Auckland, killing photographer Fernando Pereira. Ship was preparing to lead a protest flotilla to Moruroa atoll against French nuclear tests. New Zealand police arrested two agents travelling as Swiss couple Alain and Sophie Turenge, who pleaded guilty to manslaughter and received ten-year sentences. Walgate's Nature report conveyed early shock at state sabotage in a friendly port. A 1986 UN Secretary-General ruling ordered France to apologise, pay New Zealand 13 million US dollars and hold agents on Hao atoll for three years; France removed them early.

rainbow-warrior-bombing-1985.detail: Michael King's account, updated in 2014, reconstructs operation and political fallout, including resignation of French defence minister Charles Hernu. Bombing strengthened New Zealand's anti-nuclear stance, enacted in 1987 legislation banning nuclear-armed and nuclear-powered ships. Greenpeace received compensation through arbitration in 1987. Rainbow Warrior's hull was scuttled at Matauri Bay as a dive site. French testing at Moruroa and Fangataufa continued until January 1996, when Jacques Chirac ended it.

rarotonga-treaty-nuclear-free-1985.summary: On 6 August 1985, fortieth anniversary of Hiroshima, eight South Pacific Forum members led by Australia, New Zealand and Cook Islands signed South Pacific Nuclear Free Zone Treaty at Rarotonga. Parties pledged not to manufacture, acquire, station or test nuclear explosive devices and banned dumping of radioactive waste at sea within zone. Treaty entered into force in December 1986. Protocols invited nuclear powers to respect zone; Soviet Union and China signed in 1987, while France, Britain and United States waited until 1996 after France ended Moruroa tests. Zone adjoins Latin America's Tlatelolco zone and later Southeast Asian and African zones, covering much of southern hemisphere.

rarotonga-treaty-nuclear-free-1985.detail: Survival's 1987 analysis noted Australian insistence on allowing port visits and transit by nuclear-armed ships, a compromise that kept ANZUS alliance intact while New Zealand went further with its own 1987 ban. Thakur's chapter situates Rarotonga within regional reaction to French testing and Japanese plans to dump waste. Treaty built on decades of Pacific protest including Fiji's Against Testing on Moruroa movement and Nuclear Free and Independent Pacific conferences from 1975.

windows-1-1985.summary: In November 1985 Microsoft shipped Windows 1.0, a graphical layer on MS-DOS. Priced at US$99, it gave PC users a mouse-driven desktop with tiled, non-overlapping windows, cooperative multitasking of Windows programs and bundled Calculator, Paint, Notepad, a clock and the game Reversi. Reviews were lukewarm, finding it slow and short of applications, but it began Microsoft’s line of Windows releases that would dominate personal computing; Windows 2.0 followed in December 1987 with overlapping windows.

Computer History Museum, 'November 10, 1983: Microsoft Introduces Windows', This Day in History
sources.author: Computer History Museum
sources.confirms: The museum records that Microsoft announced Windows on 10 November 1983 to compete with graphical environments such as the Apple Lisa, and that after several delays Windows 1.0 became available in 1985.

windows-1-1985.detail: Windows 1.0 required 256 KB of memory, two floppy drives or a hard disk, and a graphics card. Its tiled windows were a design decision; Windows 2.0’s overlapping windows prompted Apple to sue Microsoft in 1988 over Macintosh’s look and feel, which Microsoft won. Microsoft supported Windows 1.0 for sixteen years, until December 31, 2001.

3d-printing-stereolithography-1986.summary: In 1986 Chuck Hull patented stereolithography, building objects layer by layer with light-cured resin. His machine traced each cross-section of a computer model with an ultraviolet laser across liquid photopolymer, hardening one thin layer at a time and lowering its part into resin until complete. Hull founded 3D Systems in Valencia, California, that year, shipped its first commercial printer, SLA-1, in 1987, and devised its STL file format still used in 3D printing.

sources.confirms: Hull's patent describes curing successive thin layers of liquid photopolymer with ultraviolet light to build a three-dimensional object from cross-sections.

Alain Le Méhauté, Olivier de Witte and Jean-Claude André filed a French patent three weeks before Hull, which their employers abandoned. Hull’s patent describes a concentrated ultraviolet beam focused on liquid photopolymer’s surface in its vat.

backprop-rumelhart-1986.summary: In 1986 Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams published backpropagation, the method for training deep neural networks that modern AI still uses. Their paper showed how to train neural networks with hidden layers: compute the gap between a network’s output and its target, then pass that error backward through each layer using calculus’s chain rule to find how every weight contributed, and nudge each weight to shrink it. Earlier perceptrons could learn only one layer, too weak for problems such as XOR. Their demonstration that networks could learn useful internal representations revived neural network research and underlies modern deep learning.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Backpropagation
Rumelhart, David E.; Hinton, Geoffrey E.; Williams, Ronald J., "Learning representations by back-propagating errors", Nature 323 (9 October 1986), pp. 533-536
sources.author: Rumelhart, David E.; Hinton, Geoffrey E.; Williams, Ronald J.
sources.confirms: The 1986 Nature paper describing the back-propagation procedure for training networks with hidden units by propagating output error backwards to adjust weights.
sources.qualifies: The procedure had earlier forms (Werbos 1974, Linnainmaa 1970); the record credits this paper with publishing, not inventing, it.

sources.title: Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, 'The Nobel Prize in Physics 2024: Popular science background'
sources.author: Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences
sources.confirms: The 2024 physics prize background describes Hinton's work on training multilayer networks, including backpropagation, as foundational to machine learning with artificial neural networks.

backprop-rumelhart-1986.detail: Minsky and Papert had shown single-layer perceptrons’ limits in 1969. Backpropagation’s mathematics predates Rumelhart’s paper: Seppo Linnainmaa published reverse-mode automatic differentiation in 1970, and Paul Werbos proposed applying it to neural networks in his 1974 Harvard thesis, though neither reached neural network researchers. Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams’s contribution was to popularize it and show, with examples, that gradient descent could discover representations in hidden units.

cdot-rural-exchange-1986.summary: Centre for Development of Telematics, set up in August 1984 under Sam Pitroda with a small budget and young engineers, designed digital switching equipment for Indian conditions: heat, dust, unreliable power and small villages. Its 128 line Rural Automatic Exchange (RAX), first installed at Kittur in Karnataka in 1986, needed no air conditioning and could be maintained by local staff. Licensed to dozens of Indian manufacturers, RAX and later 256 and 512 line versions connected tens of thousands of villages during 1990s, while yellow STD/PCO booths spread telephone access. C-DOT designs broke dependence on imported exchanges and trained engineers who later staffed India's telecom industry.

cfaa-1986.summary: In 1986 America's Computer Fraud and Abuse Act made accessing a “protected computer” without authorization, or exceeding authorized access, a federal crime, at first covering government and financial computers and later any computer used in interstate commerce. Its House committee report cited WarGames as “a realistic representation of the automatic dialing and access capabilities of the personal computer.” Its first prosecution convicted Robert Tappan Morris for his 1988 worm. Critics called it vague, and in 2021 a Supreme Court ruling, Van Buren v. United States, narrowed it.

sources.title: Computer Fraud and Abuse Act - Wikipedia
Computer Fraud and Abuse Act of 1986, Public Law 99-474, 100 Stat. 1213 (16 October 1986)
sources.author: United States Congress
sources.confirms: Enacted 16 October 1986, the Act amended 18 USC 1030 to create federal computer fraud and unauthorised access offences.

sources.title: Kerr, Orin S. 'Vagueness Challenges to the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act.' Minnesota Law Review 94 (2010): 1561-1587.

cfaa-1986.detail: Congress amended CFAA repeatedly, including through 2001’s Patriot Act, broadening its reach and penalties. Prosecutors used it against Aaron Swartz for downloading JSTOR articles; his suicide in 2013 prompted reform proposals known as Aaron’s Law, which did not pass. Van Buren held that a person who has access to information does not exceed authorization by using it for an improper purpose.

challenger-disaster-1986.summary: In January 1986 Challenger broke apart 73 seconds after launch, killing seven on live television. Among them was schoolteacher Christa McAuliffe, whose Teacher in Space flight had schools across America watching live. Overnight temperatures had dropped near freezing, and rubber O-rings sealing a joint in its right solid rocket booster stiffened in that cold and failed; hot gas burned through to the external fuel tank, which ruptured. Morton Thiokol engineers had recommended against launching below 53 °F the night before and were overruled. Shuttles stayed grounded for 32 months.

challenger-disaster-1986.detail: Its crew compartment survived breakup and fell into the Atlantic. NASA managers had pressed Thiokol for a signed recommendation to launch. President Reagan’s Rogers Commission found NASA’s decision process flawed; physicist Richard Feynman demonstrated O-ring brittleness on television by dipping a sample in ice water. NASA redesigned its boosters’ field joints and returned to flight with Discovery in September 1988.

picture.credit: NASA, Public domain, via NASA Image and Video Library

chernobyl-disaster-1986.summary: In 1986 a Chernobyl reactor exploded. Operators had reduced power with protective systems disabled, and its Soviet RBMK design, in which steam voids increased reactivity and control rods briefly raised power on insertion, turned an emergency shutdown into a surge; steam blew off its 1,000-tonne lid and its exposed graphite core burned for days, spreading fallout across Europe. Thirty-one people died within weeks, about 350,000 were evacuated, and it is rated Level 7, maximum on the International Nuclear Event Scale.

chernobyl-disaster-1986.detail: WHO and IAEA studies estimate about 4,000 eventual cancer deaths among those most exposed, and other assessments run much higher. Thousands of thyroid cancers were recorded in children who drank contaminated milk. A 2,600 km² exclusion zone remains. A concrete sarcophagus enclosed the ruin in 1986 and the New Safe Confinement arch covered it in 2016. Soviet authorities delayed announcing it, and Mikhail Gorbachev later said Chernobyl pushed glasnost; cleanup cost roughly 18 billion rubles.

chukha-hydro-bhutan-1986.summary: Under a 1974 agreement India funds Chukha hydroelectric project on Wangchu river in western Bhutan, 60 percent as grant and 40 percent as loan, with Indian engineers building a 336 megawatt run-of-river station of four 84 megawatt units. Commissioning runs from 1986 to 1988. Over three quarters of output is exported to India at a negotiated tariff, and electricity sales reach about 45 percent of Bhutan's national revenue during its eighth plan. This model, repeated at Kurichhu, Tala and Punatsangchhu, lets a country of under a million people fund schools and health care from rivers while domestic electrification spreads from towns to villages.

Wangdi and Richards (IEEE 1990) describe plant and grid. Grant-loan split from Indian embassy and Bhutan government documents.

cuba-cigb-biotech-1985.summary: In 1986 Cuba opened a genetic engineering centre in Havana built with its own funds; it made the country's vaccines, later its Covid shots. It grew from a 1981 Biological Front, a small group that had produced interferon that year and a 1982 Centre for Biological Research, and it put research, development and manufacture under one roof so that Cuban scientists could carry products from gene to clinic. Its laboratories went on to produce a recombinant hepatitis B vaccine, Heberprot-P for diabetic foot ulcers and, in 2021, Abdala, Cuba’s COVID-19 vaccine, exported to dozens of countries.

sources.confirms: Cuba's Centre for Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology in Havana, built with state funds in the mid-1980s, employed about 1,080 staff and produced the country's vaccines.

cuba-cigb-biotech-1985.detail: CIGB anchors Havana’s Scientific Pole and belongs to BioCubaFarma, Cuba’s state biotechnology and pharmaceutical group. Its hepatitis B vaccine was among the first recombinant vaccines made outside rich countries, and its products are exported mainly to Latin America, Asia and Africa.

engines-of-creation-gray-goo-1986.summary: In 1986 Eric Drexler's Engines of Creation imagined molecular machines and a grey goo that could eat the world. It names a scenario in which self-replicating nanomachines run out of control and consume Earth’s biomass while building more of themselves. He illustrated exponential growth with a replicator that builds one copy every thousand seconds: after ten hours over 68 billion exist, and in under two days they would outweigh Earth, were raw materials unlimited. His book gave grey goo two paragraphs and a note. Omni magazine popularized it in November 1986, and in 2004 Drexler said “I wish I had never used the term ‘gray goo’.”

sources.title: Gray goo - Wikipedia
Engines of Creation
Wikipedia: Gray goo
Drexler, K. Eric, Engines of Creation: The Coming Era of Nanotechnology
sources.author: K. Eric Drexler
sources.venue: Anchor Press / Doubleday, Garden City, NY

sources.title: Picraux, S. Tom, 'Nanotechnology', Encyclopaedia Britannica

engines-of-creation-gray-goo-1986.detail: Drexler warned that tough omnivorous “bacteria” could out-compete living ones and reduce the biosphere to dust in days. John von Neumann had described macroscopic self-replicating machines, sometimes called von Neumann machines. Sun Microsystems co-founder Bill Joy raised grey goo in his 2000 Wired essay “Why The Future Doesn’t Need Us,” and Robert Freitas published its first quantitative analysis, of ecophagy, that year. Prince Charles asked Britain’s Royal Society to investigate nanotechnology’s risks; its July 2004 report judged runaway replicators remote. Drexler argued that his term had fed fears that hampered research on conventional nanotechnology.

fluoxetine-prozac-1986.summary: In 1986 fluoxetine reached its first patients in Belgium; as Prozac it made antidepressants ordinary and sold to tens of millions. Eli Lilly had invented it in 1972 after scientist David T. Wong proposed screening compounds for their effect on reuptake of serotonin, norepinephrine and dopamine; fluoxetine proved most potent and selective at blocking serotonin reuptake, so more of that neurotransmitter stayed active between nerve cells. America’s FDA gave final approval in December 1987, Lilly began marketing Prozac a month later, and American sales reached $350 million within a year.

fluoxetine-prozac-1986.detail: Lilly filed its new drug application in 1974 and FDA accepted it in 1977. Worldwide sales peaked at $2.6 billion a year. Fluoxetine is on WHO’s List of Essential Medicines, is available as a generic, and in 2023 ranked eighteenth among medications prescribed in America.

guinea-worm-eradication-campaign-1986.summary: Dracunculiasis is caught by drinking water containing fleas that carry larvae; a year later a metre-long worm emerges through its host's skin. In 1986 an estimated 3.5 million people were infected each year in 20 countries of Africa and Asia, and the Carter Center, with CDC, WHO and UNICEF, led a campaign begun after a 1980 WHO resolution. Its tools were simple: cloth and pipe filters, larvicide Abate in ponds from 1990, village volunteers who kept emerging worms out of water, and cash rewards for reporting cases. Human cases fell to 15 in 2024 and to 10 provisional cases in 2025, in Chad, Ethiopia and South Sudan. WHO has certified 200 countries free. Infections in dogs in Chad, Cameroon and Angola remain the last obstacle to a second eradication of a human disease after smallpox.

sources.title: Hopkins, Donald R.; Weiss, Adam J.; Yerian, Sarah et al., 'Progress Toward Eradication of Dracunculiasis (Guinea Worm Disease): Worldwide, January 2024-June 2025', MMWR Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report 74 (2026)

sources.author: Carter Center
sources.confirms: Confirms 10 provisional human cases in 2025 (Chad 4, Ethiopia 4, South Sudan 2), the animal infection counts, Abate use since 1990, and the status as the second human disease to approach eradication.

guinea-worm-eradication-campaign-1986.verification_note: 2025 case totals are provisional until WHO and national programmes certify them in 2026. MMWR puts 1986's burden in 20 countries; the Carter Center says 21.

high-temperature-superconductivity-1986.summary: In 1986 Bednorz and Müller found a ceramic that superconducted at 35 kelvin, breaking a limit thought fixed; their Nobel Prize in Physics came the next year. Within months others found that swapping lanthanum for yttrium gave YBCO, superconducting above 90 K, warmer than liquid nitrogen’s 77 K boiling point.

sources.author: Bednorz, J. Georg; Müller, K. Alex
sources.venue: Zeitschrift für Physik B Condensed Matter
sources.confirms: The 1986 article by Bednorz and Müller reports an abrupt resistivity decrease interpreted as the onset of percolative superconductivity, with the highest onset temperature in the 30 K range.
sources.qualifies: The article reports an onset in the 30 K range, not an exact 35 K result.

sources.confirms: The page says Bednorz and Müller reported superconductivity in an oxide material in 1986 at a temperature 12°C higher than the previous known limit, and jointly received the 1987 Nobel Prize in Physics.

high-temperature-superconductivity-1986.detail: Liquid nitrogen is cheap and easy to handle, so high-temperature superconductors promised practical magnets, power cables and sensors, and they tolerate stronger magnetic fields than older materials. Being brittle ceramics, cuprates are hard to form into wire. Philip W. Anderson offered a first theory in 1987, and a full explanation of cuprate superconductivity is still developing.

id3-decision-trees-1986.summary: In 1986 Ross Quinlan's paper “Induction of Decision Trees” published ID3, which grows a decision tree by asking the most informative question first. Decision trees classify examples by asking about one attribute at a time. ID3 builds such trees from labelled examples: at each node it measures every unused attribute’s information gain, how much knowing that value reduces uncertainty about class, splits on whichever gains most, and repeats on each subset until examples agree or attributes run out. ID3 preceded Quinlan’s C4.5, and decision trees became standard machine learning tools.

sources.title: ID3 algorithm
Quinlan, J. R., 'Induction of Decision Trees', Machine Learning 1 (1986), pp. 81-106
sources.author: Quinlan, J. R.
sources.confirms: The 1986 paper presenting ID3, received 1 August 1985, from the New South Wales Institute of Technology.

sources.title: Hendrik Blockeel, Laurens Devos, Benoit Frenay, Geraldin Nanfack and Siegfried Nijssen, 'Decision trees: from efficient prediction to responsible AI', Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence 6 (2023) 1124553
sources.author: Hendrik Blockeel, Laurens Devos, Benoit Frenay, Geraldin Nanfack and Siegfried Nijssen
sources.confirms: This review attributes ID3 to Quinlan (1986) among the decision tree learners developed around the 1980s.

id3-decision-trees-1986.detail: Its 3 marks Quinlan’s third attempt at an entropy-based model, and “dichotomiser” is a misnomer since ID3 can split into more than two branches. Leaves are labelled with their subset’s most common class. Because ID3 is greedy, never revisiting earlier choices, it usually produces small trees but not necessarily the smallest; it can overfit training data, and continuous attributes are harder to handle than categorical ones.

kranzbergs-laws-1986.summary: In 1986 Melvin Kranzberg wrote that technology is neither good nor bad, nor is it neutral. His article, his 1985 presidential address to the Society for the History of Technology at Henry Ford Museum in Dearborn, Michigan, made this his first law: technology interacts with its social ecology, so technical developments often have environmental, social and human consequences going far beyond their devices' immediate purposes, and one technology can produce different results in different contexts. His six laws became a standard reference in technology studies.

sources.title: [PDF] Technology and History: "Kranzberg's Laws"
Melvin Kranzberg, 'Technology and History: "Kranzberg's Laws"', Technology and Culture 27 (1986)
sources.author: Kranzberg, Melvin
sources.confirms: The published presidential address setting out the six laws, including the first law that technology is neither good nor bad, nor is it neutral.

kranzbergs-laws-1986.detail:
Kranzberg illustrated unforeseen consequences with DDT. It raised farm yields and controlled disease-carrying pests while threatening ecological systems and food chains; in India, he noted, WHO reported it had cut malaria from 100 million cases a year to 15,000 and deaths from 750,000 to 1,500.

His other laws: “Invention is the mother of necessity”; “Technology comes in packages, big and small”; “Although technology might be a prime element in many public issues, nontechnical factors take precedence in technology-policy decisions”; “All history is relevant, but the history of technology is the most relevant”; and “Technology is a very human activity, and so is the history of technology.”

lake-nyos-1986.summary: On the night of 21 August 1986 a crater lake in Cameroon's Northwest Province released a dense cloud of carbon dioxide that flowed down valleys and suffocated about 1,700 people and thousands of cattle in Nyos, Cha and Subum. George Kling's team showed in 1987 that magmatic CO2 had built up in deep lake water over years and escaped when stratification overturned, a limnic eruption. A smaller event at Lake Monoun in 1984 had killed 37. Cameroonian, French and American teams installed degassing pipes from 2001 that vent deep water as a fountain, a direct engineering answer to a newly recognised hazard.

sources.author: Kling, George W.; et al.
sources.confirms: 21 August 1986; at least 1,700 dead; CO2 of magmatic origin released from deep water

sources.author: Kerr, Richard A.

lake-nyos-1986.detail: US Geological Survey investigated on site and reported in 1987. Debate between a volcanic-eruption hypothesis and a limnic-overturn hypothesis was settled in favour of the latter. Survivors described a smell of rotten eggs and loss of consciousness; cattle died standing in fields. Cameroon resettled about 4,000 survivors to camps, and a weak natural dam at Nyos's outlet remains a flood risk that Cameroon has worked to lower since 2011.

picture.alt: Lake Nyos, Cameroon, in 1986 after the gas release, with the promontory that water washed over in the foreground
picture.credit: Jack Lockwood, via Wikimedia Commons

mir-1986.summary: In February 1986 Moscow launched Mir's core; the station grew for a decade and crews lived in orbit for over a year. It formed its base block and provided resident crews’ main living quarters. Mir was history’s first modular space station: its core carried docking ports to which six further modules were attached between 1987 and 1996, each launched on its own rocket. Operated by Soviet and then Russian authorities, Mir was the first continuously inhabited long-term research station in orbit, with 3,644 days of continuous human presence before its deorbit in March 2001.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Mir
Uri, John, '35 Years Ago: Launch of Mir Space Station’s First Module', NASA (2021)
sources.author: Uri, John
sources.confirms: The page says the Soviet Union launched Mir’s base block on February 19, 1986, that it provided living accommodations, and that Mir hosted long-duration expeditions of 438, 380, and 366 days.

sources.title: Harland, David M., 'Mir | Description, Launch, History, & Facts', Encyclopaedia Britannica (2026)

sources.confirms: The page says the Soviet Union launched Mir's core module on February 20, 1986, five expansion modules were added between 1987 and 1996, and Valery Polyakov spent 438 continuous days in space.
sources.qualifies: Britannica lists five expansion modules, rather than the record’s six further modules.

mir-1986.detail: Mir had been authorised in 1976 as an improved Salyut station and was rushed into orbit ahead of the 27th Party Congress. Each arriving module first docked at Mir's forward port, then swung to its final side port by its Lyappa arm. Kvant-1 docked on 11 April 1987, followed by Kvant-2 in 1989, Kristall in 1990, Spektr in 1995 and Priroda in 1996, with a docking module delivered by Space Shuttle Atlantis in November 1995. Valeri Polyakov spent 437 days aboard from 1994 to 1995, history’s longest single spaceflight. Its continuous-presence record stood until the International Space Station passed it in 2010. Funding was cut off and Mir reentered over the Pacific near Fiji on 23 March 2001; former RKA director Yuri Koptev estimated its programme cost at $4.2 billion.

navlab-1986.summary: In 1986 Carnegie Mellon built Navlab 1, a van driven by computers that filled its back. Navlab 1 was a Chevrolet panel van carrying five racks of computer hardware, including three Sun workstations and a fridge-sized Warp supercomputer; software limits kept it from working fully until late in the decade, when it reached 20 mph. ALVINN, a neural network for autonomous navigation, was developed in 1988. Later vehicles ran to Navlab 11, and Navlab 5 steered across America in 1995.

sources.title: ALVINN
Thorpe, Charles, and Kanade, Takeo, '1986 Year End Report for Road Following at Carnegie Mellon', CMU-RI-TR-87-11 (Pittsburgh: Robotics Institute, May 1987)
sources.author: Thorpe, Charles; Kanade, Takeo
sources.confirms: The 1986 year-end report describes the Navlab, a Chevrolet van built under DARPA funding carrying five racks of computing including Sun workstations and a Warp processor.

sources.author: Kanade, Takeo, et al.
sources.confirms: The report records the design of Navlab as a robot vehicle and the first application of the Warp systolic processor.

navlab-1986.detail: Navlab 1 also carried video gear and a GPS receiver, powered by its portable 5 kW generator. ALVINN (“An Autonomous Land Vehicle in a Neural Network”) is detailed in Dean A. Pomerleau’s 1992 PhD thesis and demonstrated early representation learning, sensor fusion and data augmentation. Navlab 1 burned in 1989 when its air conditioning leaked onto its computers. In July 1995 Navlab 5, a Pontiac Trans Sport minivan, drove from Pittsburgh to San Diego on its “No Hands Across America” trip, steering autonomously for all but 50 of 2,850 miles at over 60 mph on average; it entered the Robot Hall of Fame in 2008.

nsfnet-1986.summary: In 1986 the National Science Foundation linked universities through NSFNET; the internet's backbone moved from military to academia. NSF had set it up in 1985 to connect its five supercomputing centers to each other and to regional research networks linking campuses, so that university scientists anywhere could reach those machines. It became the principal Internet backbone in summer 1986, when MIDnet, NSFNET’s first regional backbone, became operational. NSF retired its backbone in 1995, by which time it had grown into today's Internet.

sources.title: National Science Foundation Network - Wikipedia
National Science Foundation, 'Birth of the Commercial Internet', NSF and the Birth of the Internet (special report)
sources.author: National Science Foundation
sources.confirms: NSF launched NSFNET in 1986 to link researchers to its supercomputer centres and it became the de facto US internet backbone.

sources.title: B. M. Leiner, V. G. Cerf, D. D. Clark, R. E. Kahn, L. Kleinrock, D. C. Lynch, J. Postel, L. G. Roberts and S. Wolff, 'A brief history of the internet', ACM SIGCOMM Computer Communication Review 39 (2009), 22-31
sources.author: Barry M. Leiner et al.
sources.confirms: History of the internet written by its principal architects, including the NSFNET period.

nsfnet-1986.detail: Dennis Jennings led NSF’s networking program when NSFNET was established, and Colorado's National Center for Atmospheric Research was its sixth backbone site. Its routers were PDP-11/73 minicomputers running software called Fuzzballs, configured by Hans-Werner Braun at Merit Network, with Ed Krol at Illinois leading operations. Traffic from regional networks soon congested its 56 kbit/s links; NSF solicited an upgrade in June 1987, and IBM and MCI, with Merit as lead organization, won it that November. Only government agencies and universities could use NSFNET until 1989, when a first commercial Internet service provider emerged; NSF removed access restrictions in 1991 and decommissioned its fiber backbone on April 30, 1995.

nuclear-stockpile-peak-1986.summary: In 1986 the world's nuclear arsenal peaked at about 70,300 warheads; it has since fallen by more than four fifths. Most belonged to America and the Soviet Union, then in their Cold War arms race's final years. Arms control treaties and unilateral cuts then reduced global inventories to roughly 12,200 to 12,300 warheads as 2026 began. Nine countries now hold nuclear weapons; Russia and America still own about 86 percent of them, and about 3,900 warheads sit deployed with operational forces, with others in storage or awaiting dismantlement.

sources.title: Status of World Nuclear Forces (Federation of American Scientists)

nuclear-stockpile-peak-1986.detail: FAS counts about 9,745 warheads in military stockpiles available for use, with retired but intact warheads making up the rest. China, India, North Korea, Pakistan and Britain, and possibly Russia, are thought to be increasing their stockpiles, so declines since 1986 have slowed.

pdp-connectionism-1986.summary: In 1986 the Parallel Distributed Processing volumes revived neural networks, alongside Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams's Nature paper that year showing hidden layers could be trained by back-propagation. It introduced intermediate processors, now known as hidden layers, between input and output units, and sigmoid activation functions in place of the perceptron’s all-or-nothing switch, so networks could learn non-linear mappings. Connectionism’s first wave had begun with McCulloch and Pitts in 1943 and Frank Rosenblatt’s 1958 perceptron. Its second wave blossomed in the late 1980s following this publication, and its models of cognition as patterns across many simple units are ancestors of deep learning.

sources.title: Connectionism

sources.author: Rumelhart, David E.; McClelland, James L.; PDP Research Group
sources.confirms: The record identifies Parallel Distributed Processing by Rumelhart and McClelland, published by The MIT Press.
sources.qualifies: The book is dated 1986, not 1987.

sources.title: Rumelhart, David E.; Hinton, Geoffrey E.; Williams, Ronald J., 'Learning representations by back-propagating errors', Nature (1986)
sources.author: Rumelhart, David E.; Hinton, Geoffrey E.; Williams, Ronald J.
sources.confirms: The abstract describes back-propagation adjusting network weights and says hidden units come to represent important features, distinguishing the method from simpler methods such as the perceptron-convergence procedure.
sources.qualifies: This source is a 1986 Nature article, not a Parallel Distributed Processing volume.

pdp-connectionism-1986.verification_note: Rumelhart and McClelland's PDP volumes are dated 1986; back-propagation's demonstration is Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams's 1986 Nature article, not a PDP volume.
pdp-connectionism-1986.detail: Their work built on John Hopfield’s study of sigmoid activation functions’ mathematics, and discovery of non-linear activation functions is what enabled connectionism’s second wave. From the late 1980s to the mid-1990s, Schneider, Horgan and Tienson asked whether connectionism represented a fundamental shift in psychology away from “good old-fashioned AI,” and connectionism sounded near-revolutionary. Its third wave is deep learning, which made large language models possible.

society-of-mind-1986.summary: In 1986 (its first printing carries a 1985 copyright) Marvin Minsky's The Society of Mind explained intelligence as many mindless agents working together. Minsky had begun developing his theory with Seymour Papert in the early 1970s, drawing his main ideas from trying to make a robotic arm, video camera and computer stack children’s blocks. His book, published by Simon & Schuster, builds its model step by step in 270 self-contained one-page essays grouped in 30 chapters, holding that “minds are what brains do.” He later extended his theory in The Emotion Machine, and his book was also issued as a CD-ROM.

sources.title: Society of Mind (Wikipedia)
Marvin Minsky
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors
sources.confirms: Minsky's The Society of Mind presents intelligence as the product of many simple, non-intelligent agents interacting.
sources.qualifies: Dates the book to 1985.

sources.title: Lance, James W., 'If I Only Had a Brain: A Computer's Guide', New York Times, 22 February 1987
sources.author: James W. Lance
sources.confirms: Reviews Minsky's The Society of Mind (Simon and Schuster, 339 pp.), which proposes viewing the brain as an assembly of agents each mindless on their own, with each thought given its own section of about a page.

sources.title: Minsky, Marvin, 'Genius May Be More Common Than You Think' (excerpt from The Society of Mind), Los Angeles Times, 7 December 1986
sources.author: Marvin Minsky
sources.confirms: An excerpt from The Society of Mind, copyright 1986 by Marvin Minsky, described as to be published the following month by Simon and Schuster.
sources.qualifies: Places publication at the turn of 1986 to 1987.

society-of-mind-1986.verification_note: Britannica dates Minsky's book to 1985, and Simon and Schuster's first printing carries a 1985 copyright; a Los Angeles Times extract of 7 December 1986 carries a 1986 copyright and says it was 'to be published next month', reviews appeared in January and February 1987, and its trade edition is usually cited as 1986. Reviews confirm its agents thesis.
society-of-mind-1986.detail: Minsky’s agents are individually simple processes, fundamental thinking entities from which minds are built. Together they produce whatever abilities people attribute to minds, and his theory treats any naturally evolved cognitive system in this way. Block-stacking revealed how many small competences such play demands. His book was his theory’s first comprehensive statement; each essay is self-contained. Simon & Schuster published it, and it was also issued as a CD-ROM.

subsumption-architecture-1986.summary: In 1986 Rodney Brooks built robots with no model of the world, just layered reflexes; his insect robots became the Roomba. Disappointed with robots that built internal models of the world before acting, Brooks decomposed behavior into layers, each a module for one goal such as “avoid an object” or “wander around,” running at once with no central control; higher layers subsume lower ones by inhibiting or suppressing their signals, so robots react within human-like time. Brooks held that “the world is its own best model,” and his robots Allen, Herbert and Genghis shaped behavior-based robotics through the 1980s and 1990s.

sources.title: Subsumption architecture
Brooks, Rodney A., "A robust layered control system for a mobile robot", IEEE Journal on Robotics and Automation 2, no. 1 (1986), pp. 14-23
sources.author: Brooks, Rodney A.
sources.venue: IEEE Journal on Robotics and Automation
sources.confirms: Brooks's original paper proposing layered task-achieving behaviours (the subsumption architecture) in place of a central world model.

sources.title: Brooks, Rodney A., 'Intelligence without representation', Artificial Intelligence 47, no. 1-3 (1991): 139-159
sources.author: Brooks, Rodney A.
sources.confirms: Brooks's paper arguing, from the series of mobile robots his MIT group built to operate as Creatures in office environments, that intelligence can be decomposed into parallel activity-producing layers without central representations.

subsumption-architecture-1986.detail: Brooks had been disappointed with Shakey the robot and other representation-based projects. Each layer is a set of augmented finite-state machines that continuously and asynchronously read sensors and send signals; inhibition blocks signals from reaching actuators, suppression replaces inputs to a layer. Designers build and debug their lowest layer first, then add another with its suppression and inhibition connections, repeating for as many behaviors as needed. Brooks argued that embodiment forces designers to build control systems that work in physical surroundings and grounds symbols directly in sense data, and that perception and mobility are necessary foundations for human-like intelligence. Herbert collected soda cans; Genghis was a six-legged walker.

us-japan-semiconductor-agreement-1986.summary: In 1986 Japan agreed to limit chip exports and open its market after passing America in memory chips. That year's US-Japan Semiconductor Agreement capped DRAM export volumes and prices to America and required Japan to import more US chips. Japanese chips were then cheaper and better than American ones, and six of ten leading global chipmakers were Japanese. None remains in that top ten today, and in Hankyoreh columnist Ahn Seon-hee’s words, “the void left by Japan was filled by Korea.”

sources.title: [Column] The 40-year-old agreement haunting Korea's ...
Irwin, Douglas A., 'Trade Politics and the Semiconductor Industry', in Anne O. Krueger, ed., The Political Economy of American Trade Policy (University of Chicago Press, 1996), pp. 11-72
sources.author: Irwin, Douglas A.
sources.confirms: The US-Japan Semiconductor Trade Arrangement was reached on 30 July 1986 and signed 2 September 1986, setting company-specific price floors and a foreign market share target.

us-japan-semiconductor-agreement-1986.detail: Japan's six firms in that 1980s top ten were NEC, Toshiba, Hitachi, Fujitsu, Mitsubishi Electric and Matsushita Electric. Ahn’s 2026 column reads SK Group chairman Chey Tae-won’s warning that Korea could “follow in the footsteps of Japan” as a reference to this agreement, since Samsung and SK Hynix now face similar American pressure. She contrasts two eras: in the 1980s cheaper, better Japanese chips were displacing American products, while today prices are soaring amid a global supply deficit, and American anxiety about depending on foreign memory makers has shifted from Japan to Korea and Taiwan.

azt-first-hiv-drug-1987.summary: In March 1987 FDA approved AZT, the first drug for HIV, after a placebo-controlled trial was stopped early because treated patients lived longer. Jerome Horwitz had synthesized AZT in 1964 as a possible cancer drug and shelved it when it proved inert in mice; in February 1985, National Cancer Institute scientists screening compounds found that it blocked HIV in cell cultures, and approval came 25 months after that finding. A nucleoside analog, it jams an enzyme HIV uses to copy its genes into cellular DNA, slowing replication.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Zidovudine

sources.author: Fischl, Margaret A.; Richman, Douglas D.; Grieco, Michael H.; Gottlieb, Michael S.; Volberding, Paul A.; et al.

sources.author: Broder, Samuel
sources.confirms: Peer-reviewed history by the NCI researcher who led AZT's laboratory testing, recording that zidovudine (AZT), first given to patients in 1985, was the first antiretroviral drug approved by the FDA.

azt-first-hiv-drug-1987.detail: France's Institut Pasteur had identified HIV in 1983. NCI’s Samuel Broder, Hiroaki Mitsuya and Robert Yarchoan ran that screening program, and Burroughs Wellcome, which had begun its own program in June 1984, ran its placebo-controlled trial. An FDA advisory panel voted ten to one to recommend approval. Early patients took 400 mg every four hours, day and night, against 300 mg twice daily today. AZT alone cannot stop replication and HIV evolves resistance by mutating its reverse transcriptase, so from the mid-1990s it was given in combinations known as highly active antiretroviral therapy. It was approved for infants and children in 1990, and from 1994 to 1999 it was the main means of preventing mother-to-child transmission in America.

cairo-metro-line-1-opens-1987.summary: Egypt's National Authority for Tunnels opens Line 1 of Cairo Metro on 27 September 1987, running from Helwan in south to Ramses station in centre by joining two suburban railways through a new 4.7 kilometre tunnel under downtown. French consortium led by SOFRETU designs and builds it with soft-loan finance; Egyptian crews later run and extend it to El Marg in 1989. It carries over a million riders a day within a few years. Two further lines follow, one with Japanese finance, and system shapes commuting for a metropolis heading past 20 million. Later studies examine how it changed daily habits, from women-only cars to vendor economies at stations.

darpa-cuts-1987.summary: In 1987 DARPA's new computing chief, Jack Schwarz, dismissed expert systems as clever programming and cut AI funding. SCI had spent $100 million by 1985, with 92 projects underway at 60 institutions, half in industry and half in universities and government labs. Schwarz held that DARPA should back only technologies showing most promise, should “surf” rather than “dog paddle,” and that AI was not “the next wave”; his cuts, described as eviscerating SCI, ended new AI spending by 1988 and helped bring on the second AI winter.

sources.title: Review of Roland and Shiman, Strategic Computing

darpa-cuts-1987.detail: Program insiders cited problems of communication, organization and integration among its projects. Several projects survived, among them its pilot’s assistant and autonomous land vehicle, though neither was delivered.

era-winter2.summary: From 1987 the market for AI hardware collapsed and expert systems proved brittle; funding dried up again for a decade. By 1985 corporations were spending over a billion dollars a year on AI, mostly on in-house expert systems, and software firms and Lisp computer makers had grown up to serve them. Then general-purpose workstations undercut Lisp machines, expert systems proved costly to maintain, and DARPA cut its AI budget. This dataset ends its span in 1993, when its statistical era begins, so both overlap in reality.

sources.title: AI winter

sources.author: Hendler, James
sources.confirms: Describes the late-1980s AI winter when the Lisp machine market collapsed, expert systems proved brittle and DARPA cut funding.

sources.confirms: University-press history covering the expert-systems boom, the collapse of the Lisp machine companies and the funding retrenchment from 1987.

era-winter2.detail: Digital Equipment’s XCON, which configured computer orders, was the best-known in-house expert system. Hardware companies Symbolics and LISP Machines Inc. and software firms such as Teknowledge and Intellicorp had grown up around expert systems; Sun workstations running Lucid’s Lisp displaced their machines. By the early 1990s most commercial Lisp companies had failed and Texas Instruments and Xerox had left the field. Enthusiasm for AI reached its low point in the early 1990s and has generally increased since, with investment rising sharply from about 2012.

eureka-prometheus-1987.summary: In 1987 Europe funded PROMETHEUS, a €750 million driverless car programme; by 1994 its cars drove themselves on a Paris motorway. It received €749,000,000 in funding from EUREKA member states, making it the largest research project ever in driverless cars, with upwards of 600 companies taking part. Ernst Dickmanns and his team at Bundeswehr Universität München collaborated with Daimler-Benz; in 1994 their VaMP and VITA-2 vehicles drove more than 1,000 kilometres on a Paris highway in standard traffic at up to 130 kilometres per hour, steering by camera vision and changing lanes to pass other cars.

sources.title: Eureka Prometheus Project
Dickmanns, Ernst D., 'Computer Vision and Highway Automation', Vehicle System Dynamics 31 (1999) 325-343
sources.author: Dickmanns, Ernst D.
sources.confirms: The EUREKA PROMETHEUS programme (1987 to 1994) and its 1994 autonomous drives near Paris, described by the lead researcher.

sources.title: Ernst D. Dickmanns, 'The development of machine vision for road vehicles in the last decade', IEEE Intelligent Vehicle Symposium 2002, 268-281
sources.author: Ernst D. Dickmanns
sources.confirms: Crossref metadata confirms Dickmanns's retrospective on a decade of road vehicle vision, covering the PROMETHEUS demonstrations; the IEEE page would not open.

eureka-prometheus-1987.detail: Participants included BMW, Bosch, Fiat, Mercedes, Peugeot, Renault, Siemens, Volkswagen and Volvo. Its culminating Board Members Meeting in Paris on 18 to 20 October 1994 showed Common European Demonstrators from across its sub-projects. In 1987 some British universities had objected that its industrial focus neglected traffic safety issues such as pedestrian protection. Dickmanns’s twin robot cars demonstrated driving in free lanes, convoy driving, automatic tracking of other vehicles, and lane changes left and right with autonomous passing, and PROMETHEUS defined the state of the art in autonomous vehicles for its decade.

goiania-caesium-137-accident-1987.summary: On 13 September 1987 two men removed a teletherapy head from an abandoned radiotherapy clinic in Goiânia, capital of Goiás, and sold it to scrapyard owner Devair Ferreira. Workers broke open a capsule holding about 93 grams of caesium-137 chloride, 50.9 terabecquerels, and the glowing blue powder passed among family and neighbours for two weeks. Doctors recognised radiation sickness on 28 September; four people died, including six-year-old Leide das Neves Ferreira, 249 were found contaminated, and about 112,000 were screened in a stadium. Seven houses were demolished and 3,500 cubic metres of waste were sealed in a repository at Abadia de Goiás. The IAEA's 1988 report made Goiânia the reference case for orphan radioactive sources.

sources.confirms: Source activity, sequence of events, casualties, screening numbers and waste volumes.

sources.author: Godoy, J. M.; Guimarães, J. R. D.; Pereira, J. C. A.; Pires do Rio, M. A.
sources.confirms: Environmental dispersal of caesium in the city.

sources.author: Simons, Marlise
sources.confirms: First deaths, 243 affected at that date and the scrap dealer's role.

goiania-caesium-137-accident-1987.detail: Researchers traced caesium in Goiânia's waterways, and doctors treated internal contamination with Prussian blue. Goods from Goiás were boycotted across Brazil and hotels refused residents, a 'radiophobia' later studied by social scientists. The clinic's owners and a technician were convicted of negligence in 1996; Brazil's nuclear commission CNEN was criticised for weak source control.
