human-genome-project-launch-1990.detail:
US planning began in 1984; James Watson headed NIH’s genome centre, later renamed the National Human Genome Research Institute. Geneticists in Britain, France, Australia, China and elsewhere joined; funding came from NIH and many groups worldwide.

In 1998 Craig Venter’s Celera Genomics began a $300 million private effort meant to cost a fraction of public spending. Public consortium members released data daily under their 1996 Bermuda Statement and were pushed to publish their draft first; Bill Clinton and Tony Blair announced it jointly, assembled at UC Santa Cruz by Jim Kent and David Haussler, and papers followed in February 2001. Protein-coding gene estimates were later revised down to about 19,000 to 20,000, and January 2022 brought a gapless sequence of 22 autosomes plus the X chromosome.

ibm-statistical-mt-1988.summary: In 1990 IBM researchers translated French to English by statistics alone, learned from Canadian parliament records. They treated translation as probability rather than grammar rules: for each French sentence, pick the English sentence whose likelihood as English (a language model) times its likelihood of yielding that French (a translation model) is highest. Trained on Canadian Hansard proceedings, their system translated 73 French test sentences, with 48 percent judged reasonable.

sources.title: [PDF] A STATISTICAL APPROACH TO MACHINE TRANSLATION

Brown, Peter F.; Della Pietra, Stephen A.; Della Pietra, Vincent J.; Mercer, Robert L., 'The Mathematics of Statistical Machine Translation: Parameter Estimation', Computational Linguistics 19, no. 2 (1993): 263-311
sources.author: Brown, Peter F.; Della Pietra, Stephen A.; Della Pietra, Vincent J.; Mercer, Robert L.
sources.confirms: The IBM group's full account of the five translation models it had introduced from 1988, trained on Canadian Hansard French and English text.

ibm-statistical-mt-1988.detail:
The authors, at IBM’s Thomas J. Watson Research Center, revived Warren Weaver’s 1949 suggestion to attack translation “with statistical methods and ideas from information theory,” an idea researchers had soon abandoned. They argued that limited computing power and scarce machine-readable text had been the obstacles. From about 100 million words of English Hansard text and its French counterpart they extracted about three million sentence pairs with an algorithm based on sentence length, about 99 percent of them true translations.

Their experiment used English’s 1,000 most frequent words and 1,700 French words, trained a translation model with 17 million parameters on 117,000 sentence pairs, and trained its language model on 570,000 English sentences of about 12 million words. Of 73 test sentences, 4 were exact (5 percent), 18 alternate (25 percent), 13 different but legitimate (18 percent), 11 wrong (15 percent) and 27 ungrammatical (37 percent).

symbol-grounding-1990.summary: In 1990 Stevan Harnad asked how symbols a computer shuffles can mean anything; the question returned with language models. Computers shuffle tokens by formal rules, so Harnad asked how their meanings could be grounded “in anything but other meaningless symbols.” It resembles looking up words in a dictionary of a language you do not know: each definition leads only to more unknown words. Harnad argued grounding must be sensorimotor, tied to how a system perceives and acts on objects, to avoid infinite regress, and he connected this to John Searle’s 1980 Chinese Room argument.

sources.title: Symbol grounding problem (Wikipedia)
Harnad, Stevan, "The symbol grounding problem", Physica D: Nonlinear Phenomena 42, nos. 1-3 (1990), pp. 335-346
sources.author: Harnad, Stevan
sources.confirms: Harnad's original paper asking how the meanings of symbols in a formal system can be grounded in anything but other symbols.

sources.title: Taddeo, Mariarosaria, and Luciano Floridi. 'Solving the Symbol Grounding Problem: A Critical Review of Fifteen Years of Research.' Journal of Experimental and Theoretical Artificial Intelligence 17, no. 4 (2005): 419-445.
sources.author: Mariarosaria Taddeo; Luciano Floridi
sources.venue: Journal of Experimental and Theoretical Artificial Intelligence
sources.confirms: Peer-reviewed review of the research that followed Harnad's 1990 formulation of the symbol grounding problem; Crossref metadata confirmed, publisher page blocked.

symbol-grounding-1990.detail:
Harnad defined a symbol system as “a set of arbitrary ‘physical tokens’ scratches on paper, holes on a tape, events in a digital computer, etc. that are ... manipulated on the basis of ‘explicit rules’ that are ... likewise physical tokens and strings of tokens.” He framed his task as making such systems’ semantic interpretation “intrinsic to the system, rather than just parasitic on the meanings in our heads.”

He suggested two properties for grounding: capacity to pick out referents of category names through sensorimotor interaction, which cognitive science could in principle explain, and consciousness, whose independent role he considered probably insoluble “except on pain of telekinetic dualism.” His paper appeared in Physica D, volume 42, pages 335 to 346.

telmex-privatization-1990.summary: In 1990 Mexico sold a controlling 20.4 percent stake in Telmex to a group led by Carlos Slim; the monopoly made him the richest man on Earth. Telmex was described as Mexico’s dominant fixed-line phone carrier in 2014. Telmex had become Mexico’s only telephone provider after absorbing ITT’s Mexican branch, and Mexico’s government had bought a 51 percent share in 1972. Slim’s group made the largest tender, though, controversially, payment was spread over several years using phone-service revenues; the government sold its remaining stock in 1991. Its mobile spin-off América Móvil, created in 2000, later bought Telmex outright.

telmex-privatization-1990.detail:
After privatisation Telmex built a partial fibre-optic network reaching 30 percent of Mexican territory. In the 1990s it formed Radio Móvil Dipsa to provide mobile service under its Telcel brand; América Móvil, spun off in 2000, started with 80 percent of Mexico’s mobile market. América Móvil bought 60 percent of Telmex in 2010 for over 23 billion dollars and its remaining 40 percent in 2011, then began delisting Telmex from Mexico’s stock exchange in August 2012.

Telmex became an Internet provider in the mid-1990s under its Uninet brand, bought Prodigy Communications in 1996, and by 2005 held more than 80 percent of Mexico’s ISP market while leading broadband access with Prodigy Infinitum.

2g-digital-cellular-1991.summary: In 1991 the first digital cellular networks opened; phones could send text messages and calls stopped being easy to overhear. Earlier systems sent voice between handsets and base stations as analog radio signals. Converting speech to digital data let 2G networks encrypt conversations between phone and base station, fit more users into each frequency band, and carry SMS text messages. Radiolinja in Finland made the first commercial 2G launch in 1991 using GSM, defined by the European Telecommunications Standards Institute; 3G later brought higher data rates and mobile internet.

sources.title: 2G (Wikipedia)
S. Karlsson and A. Lugn, 'Who was first?', Ericsson history
sources.author: Svenolof Karlsson; Anders Lugn
sources.confirms: Radiolinja in Finland launched commercial GSM service on 1 July 1991, the day Mannesmann also declared readiness in Germany.

sources.title: Dunnewijk, Theo, and Staffan Hulten. 'A Brief History of Mobile Communication in Europe.' Telematics and Informatics 24, no. 3 (2007): 164-179.
sources.author: Theo Dunnewijk; Staffan Hulten
sources.confirms: Independent peer-reviewed history covering the move from analog NMT to the digital GSM networks that opened in 1991; Crossref metadata confirmed, Elsevier page did not open.

2g-digital-cellular-1991.detail:
Those first-generation networks were retrospectively called 1G. Other 2G technologies included cdmaOne (IS-95), defined by the Telecommunications Industry Association with an eight to tenfold increase in voice capacity over analog AMPS and first deployed in 1995; the now-discontinued Digital AMPS (IS-54 and IS-136) in North America; and Japan’s Personal Digital Cellular and Personal Handy-phone System. In 1990 AT&T Bell Labs engineers Jesse Russell, Farhad Barzegar and Can A. Eryaman filed a patent for a digital mobile phone supporting data transmission. Later additions such as General Packet Radio Service (GPRS) brought packet data for email and limited internet access, and text messaging expanded to Multimedia Messaging Service (MMS).

Carriers in the United States, Japan, Australia and elsewhere have been shutting 2G down, though some keep it as a fallback: Vodafone switched off 3G across Europe in 2020 while retaining 2G, and T-Mobile US decommissioned its 2G GSM network on August 3, 2026.

abacc-argentina-brazil-nuclear-1991.summary: On 18 July 1991 presidents Carlos Menem and Fernando Collor signed in Guadalajara, Mexico, an agreement for exclusively peaceful use of nuclear energy, committing both states to a Common System of Accounting and Control and creating Agência Brasileiro-Argentina de Contabilidade e Controle de Materiais Nucleares, based in Rio de Janeiro. Inspectors from each country verify the other's enrichment plants at Pilcaniyeu and Resende, reactors and fuel facilities, and a December 1991 Quadripartite Agreement brought IAEA into the arrangement. It capped a rapprochement begun with 1985 Foz do Iguaçu declaration and mutual site visits, ended a rivalry between two states that had kept Tlatelolco from full force, and gave both a path into the treaty, which they completed in 1994.

sources.confirms: Agreement signed in Guadalajara on 18 July 1991 by Menem and Collor; creation of ABACC and SCCC.

abacc-argentina-brazil-nuclear-1991.detail: Carasales, Argentine negotiator, describes the sequence in Nonproliferation Review; Redick, Carasales and Wrobel in Washington Quarterly set out ABACC as a regional model for mutual verification. ABACC remains the only bilateral safeguards agency of its kind. Both states had secret programmes in the 1980s: Argentina announced gaseous diffusion enrichment at Pilcaniyeu in 1983, and Brazil's navy ran centrifuge work at Aramar. Democratic transitions and economic crises made cooperation attractive; presidents Alfonsín and Sarney visited each other's facilities in 1987 and 1988. ABACC employs inspectors from both countries who audit each other's material inventories.

arxiv-1991.summary: In 1991 Paul Ginsparg started arXiv so physicists could share papers before journals printed them. Around 1990 Joanne Cohn had been e-mailing physics preprints to colleagues as compact TeX files until their volume filled mailboxes; Ginsparg saw that central storage was needed and set up a repository mailbox at Los Alamos National Laboratory. Papers are moderated but not peer reviewed. arXiv passed one million articles at the end of 2014 and two million at the end of 2021.

sources.title: ArXiv (Wikipedia)
ArXiv at 20
sources.author: Ginsparg, Paul
sources.confirms: Ginsparg's own account of starting the preprint server at Los Alamos in August 1991, prompted by Joanne Cohn's e-mail distribution lists.

sources.title: Jackson, Allyn, 'From Preprints to E-prints: The Rise of Electronic Preprint Servers in Mathematics', Notices of the American Mathematical Society 49, no. 1 (2002): 23-32
sources.author: Jackson, Allyn

sources.confirms: Independent account that Ginsparg's hep-th preprint server went online at Los Alamos National Laboratory in August 1991, operating by e-mail and ftp, and grew into the arXiv.

arxiv-1991.detail:
arXiv began as the LANL preprint archive at xxx.lanl.gov, reachable from any computer. It gained FTP access in 1991, Gopher in 1992 and Web access in 1993, and the term e-print was soon adopted for its articles. Because Los Alamos showed little interest in the expanding service, Ginsparg moved to Cornell University in 2001; Cornell University Library took administrative and financial responsibility in September 2011, and in March 2026 arXiv announced it would separate from Cornell. Ginsparg received a MacArthur Fellowship in 2002 for establishing it, joking to the Chronicle of Higher Education that it “was supposed to be a three-hour tour, not a life sentence”.

Its annual budget was about $826,000 for 2013 to 2017, funded by Cornell University Library, the Simons Foundation and fees from about 220 member institutions. In many areas of mathematics and physics almost all papers are self-archived there before journal publication; Nature named it in January 2021 among “10 computer codes that transformed science.” As of October 2026 submissions run about 32,000 articles per month.

carbon-nanotubes-1991.summary: In November 1991 Sumio Iijima at NEC reported tubes of carbon a few atoms wide; nanotechnology had a material, though such tubes had been imaged in 1952 and 1976. Electron microscopy showed each needle held 2 to about 50 coaxial tubes, and the paper set off worldwide nanotube research. Carbon nanotubes can be pictured as two-dimensional graphene sheets rolled into hollow cylinders; single-walled tubes measure about 0.5 to 2 nanometres across, roughly 100,000th of a human hair’s width, and nested tubes form the multi-walled kind Iijima found in soot from arc-burned graphite rods.

sources.title: Carbon nanotube - Wikipedia
Helical microtubules of graphitic carbon - Nature
Monthioux, Marc, and Vladimir L. Kuznetsov. 'Who Should Be Given the Credit for the Discovery of Carbon Nanotubes?' Carbon 44, no. 9 (2006): 1621-1623.
sources.author: Marc Monthioux; Vladimir L. Kuznetsov
sources.confirms: Editorial in the field's main journal reviewing the record of nanotube discovery around Iijima's 1991 Nature paper; Crossref metadata confirmed, Elsevier page did not open.
sources.qualifies: Argues that carbon nanotubes were observed in 1952 and 1976 and that Iijima's 1991 paper deserves credit for launching the field rather than for the first observation.

carbon-nanotubes-1991.verification_note: Monthioux and Kuznetsov (Carbon 2006) show hollow carbon nanofilaments were imaged by Radushkevich and Lukyanovich in 1952 and by Oberlin, Endo and Koyama in 1976; Iijima's 1991 paper is credited with starting this field, not with first observation.
carbon-nanotubes-1991.detail:
Nanotubes’ structure and strong carbon bonds give exceptional tensile strength and thermal conductivity. L. V. Radushkevich and V. M. Lukyanovich published clear images of 50-nanometre carbon tubes in the Journal of Physical Chemistry of Russia in 1952, largely unnoticed because their article was in Russian during the Cold War, and Oberlin, Endo and Koyama observed hollow tubes of rolled graphite in 1976. Marc Monthioux and Vladimir Kuznetsov argued in a 2006 editorial that Iijima’s paper earns credit for launching nanotube research and those earlier groups for first observation.

Iijima’s 1991 paper, together with Mintmire, Dunlap and White’s independent prediction that single-walled tubes would show remarkable conducting properties, created the initial excitement. In 1993 Iijima and Ichihashi at NEC and Bethune’s team at IBM independently found that adding transition-metal catalysts such as iron and cobalt to the arc discharge produced single-walled nanotubes; Thess’s team then raised yield and purity by vaporising carbon and metal in a high-temperature furnace. Some single-walled structures conduct like metals while others are semiconductors, and expected uses span electronics, optics, composite materials and nanomedicine.

gambia-bednet-trial-1991.summary: Pedro Alonso and Brian Greenwood's team at Britain's Medical Research Council laboratories in Farafenni, with Gambia's primary health care programme, treated existing village bed nets with permethrin and gave chemoprophylaxis to children in 17 villages in 1988-89, against 56 comparison villages. Mortality in children aged one to four fell to 37 percent of control levels. Published in June 1991, this was the first randomised evidence that treated nets save lives, and it led to Gambia's national programme and to trials in Ghana, Kenya and Burkina Faso that confirmed similar gains. Treated nets became a core malaria intervention worldwide.

sources.author: Alonso, Pedro L.; Lindsay, S. W.; Armstrong, J. R. M.; et al.
sources.confirms: Permethrin-treated nets plus chemoprophylaxis in 17 villages; mortality in 1-4 year olds 37 percent of controls

gambia-bednet-trial-1991.verification_note: Original trial combined nets with chemoprophylaxis, so attribution to nets alone rests on later trials; Cochrane review page confirms pooled effect.
gambia-bednet-trial-1991.detail: Nets were already common in Gambian villages, so researchers tested treatment of nets villagers owned rather than new distribution. Later multi-country trials under WHO/TDR showed roughly one in five child deaths averted. Study villages lay along Gambia's river in Farafenni area, where Medical Research Council had run field stations since 1947. Follow-up studies in Gambia measured net durability and insecticide loss after washing, informing later long-lasting net designs used in mass campaigns after 2005.

great-man-made-river-phase-1-1991.summary: On 28 August 1991 water from wellfields at Sarir and Tazirbu, drawn from Nubian Sandstone Aquifer about 500 metres down, reaches Benghazi through 4 metre diameter prestressed concrete pipe laid across 1,600 kilometres of desert. Phase I of Great Man-Made River Project, designed by Brown & Root and built mainly by Dong Ah of South Korea, carries 2 million cubic metres a day. Pipe sections are cast at Brega and Sarir in purpose-built factories; a Phase II line to Tripoli follows in 1996. Project is financed from oil revenue and framed by Gaddafi's government as eighth wonder, while hydrogeologists warn aquifer is non-renewable. Pumping continues through 2011 war and later sabotage, and most Libyan cities now depend on it.

gsm-first-call-1991.summary: On 1 July 1991, by Radiolinja's and Nokia's account, the first GSM call was made in Finland; scholarly histories confirm only a 1991 to 1992 launch period. One digital standard let a phone work across Europe and then worldwide. In 2021, former Nokia engineer Pekka Lonka said he had made a test call a couple of hours earlier, calling Marjo Jousinen in Salo. GSM, Europe’s digital cellular standard, grew from Groupe Spécial Mobile, which European postal and telecoms administrations set up in 1983 to design a common European system. Holkeri was Finland’s former prime minister and Suonio deputy mayor of Tampere.

sources.title: Wikipedia: GSM
Hillebrand, Friedhelm, 'GSM's Achievements', in Friedhelm Hillebrand, ed., GSM and UMTS: The Creation of Global Mobile Communication (Wiley, 2001)
sources.author: Hillebrand, Friedhelm
sources.confirms: GSM networks opened commercially in 1991 to 1992 after the standard was frozen, with Finland's Radiolinja among the first operators.

sources.author: Haug, Thomas

gsm-first-call-1991.detail:
Holkeri’s network was built by Nokia and Siemens and operated by Radiolinja. France and Germany signed a joint development agreement in 1984, joined by Italy and Britain in 1986. That year the European Commission proposed reserving the 900 MHz band for GSM, and in February 1987 Europe produced its first agreed GSM Technical Specification. Representatives of 13 countries signed a memorandum of understanding in Copenhagen in September 1987 to deploy it, and EU rules made GSM mandatory, producing a unified open network larger than America’s. SMS text messaging followed in 1992.

GSM became the global standard for mobile cellular communications, with over 2 billion subscribers in 2006, far above competing CDMA, and over 90 percent market share by the mid-2010s across more than 219 countries and territories. Its specifications passed in 2000 to 3GPP, which went on to develop 3G UMTS, 4G LTE Advanced and 5G; carriers began shutting GSM networks down from the late 2010s. Lonka made his claim to Helsingin Sanomat, Finland’s largest newspaper.

picture.credit: Jkbw, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

hpca-1991.summary: In December 1991 Al Gore's High Performance Computing Act funded a national research network; that money built NCSA's Mosaic browser. Enacted on December 9, 1991 and often called the Gore Bill, it extended federal networking efforts running from 1960s ARPANET to 1980s NSFNET. Its roughly $600 million funded NREN, its National Research and Education Network, and its High-Performance Computing and Communications Program, and led to Gore's National Information Infrastructure, his “Information superhighway.”

hpca-1991.detail: Funding also reached NCSA, Illinois's National Center for Supercomputing Applications, where Netscape founder Marc Andreessen’s team created Mosaic in 1993. President Bush predicted it would help reveal DNA's secrets.

kuwait-oil-well-fires-1991.summary: Iraqi troops withdrawing in February 1991 blow wellheads across Burgan, Ahmadi and northern fields, igniting more than 600 wells and leaving others gushing into lakes of crude. Plumes consume an estimated 4 to 6 million barrels a day, darken noon skies over Kuwait City and deposit soot as far as Himalayan snow, while early forecasts of a nuclear-winter effect prove wrong because smoke stays below six kilometres. Texas firms Red Adair, Boots and Coots and Wild Well Control, joined by Hungarian, Iranian, Chinese and Kuwaiti crews, use seawater pipelines, explosives and a MiG-21 engine mounted on a tank to blow out flames; Kuwait Oil Company caps its final well on 6 November 1991, months ahead of forecasts. Oil lakes and tarcrete still cover about 100 square kilometres.

linux-1991.summary: On 17 September 1991 Linus Torvalds released Linux, free software that now runs most of the internet's servers and every Android phone. Richard Stallman’s GNU Project had been building a free, Unix-compatible operating system since 1983, but its own kernel, GNU Hurd, was stalled, and Minix, written for teaching, carried licence terms that were not entirely free. Torvalds developed Linux on Minix as a fresh re-implementation containing no Unix code and released it under GNU’s GPL copyleft licence. Combined with GNU and other software it formed complete systems, and Linux now runs most web servers and supercomputers.

sources.title: Linux - Wikipedia
Torvalds, Linus, "The Linux edge", Communications of the ACM 42, no. 4 (1999), pp. 38-39
sources.author: Torvalds, Linus
sources.confirms: Torvalds's own account of starting Linux in 1991 as a Minix-inspired kernel and of its development model.
sources.qualifies: The 17 September 1991 release date of version 0.01 is from the kernel archives and Torvalds's comp.os.minix posts.

linux-1991.detail:
Linux runs over 96 percent of the top million web servers and, as of November 2017, all 500 fastest supercomputers. 386BSD, the first entirely free Unix for personal computers, did not appear until 1992, by which time Torvalds had already released Linux. Like GNU and 386BSD, Linux contained no Unix code and so avoided legal trouble with AT&T. Torvalds had asked the comp.os.minix newsgroup for POSIX standards documentation and, not finding it, worked out system calls from SunOS manuals and Andrew Tanenbaum’s Minix text; GNU applications later replaced every Minix component.

Distributions bundling the kernel with GNU, X.Org and other software brought Unix technology to home users in the 1990s, and Android uses a Linux-based kernel; together they have the largest installed base of general-purpose operating systems. Adoption beyond hobbyists began in mid-1990s supercomputing, where NASA replaced expensive machines with clusters of cheap commodity computers running Linux, and Dell, IBM and then Hewlett-Packard began offering Linux support. The kernel is licensed under GPLv2 with an exception for system calls.

picture.alt: Linus Torvalds, who released first Linux kernel in 1991, speaking at LinuxCon Europe in Dusseldorf in 2014
picture.credit: Krd, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

lithium-ion-battery-sony-1991.summary: In 1991 Sony sold the first lithium-ion batteries, and phones, laptops and electric cars became possible. Its cells store energy by shuttling lithium ions into and out of solid electrodes: John B. Goodenough introduced a lithium cobalt oxide cathode in 1980, and Yoshino's 1985 prototype used a carbon anode instead of lithium metal. In 2019 M. Stanley Whittingham, Goodenough and Yoshino won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for this work.

sources.author: Olof Ramstrom
sources.confirms: A commercial lithium-ion battery with a petroleum-coke anode and LiCoO2 cathode was released in 1991, following Yoshino's design.
sources.qualifies: Does not name Sony as the maker.

sources.author: John B. Goodenough and Kyu-Sung Park

lithium-ion-battery-sony-1991.detail:
Yoshino’s prototype was commercialised by a Sony and Asahi Kasei team led by Yoshio Nishi. That shuttling is called intercalation; Whittingham conceived intercalation electrodes in the 1970s, and his first rechargeable lithium cell paired a titanium disulfide cathode with a lithium-aluminium anode, had safety problems and never sold. Li-ion cells typically carry a nominal 3.6 or 3.7 volts and offer higher specific energy, energy density and efficiency and longer cycle and calendar life than other rechargeable types.

Their flammable electrolytes make them fire and explosion hazards: lithium plating on negative electrodes can grow dendrites that pierce separators and short-circuit cells, and in 2006 about 10 million Sony laptop batteries were recalled. Global demand passed 1 terawatt-hour per year in late 2024, with production capacity more than twice that; uses extend to grid-scale storage and military and aerospace applications.

loebner-prize-1991.summary: In 1991 the first Loebner Prize, held at Boston's Computer Museum on 8 November, went to Joseph Weintraub's PC Therapist, a chatbot limited to whimsical conversation. Hugh Loebner launched this annual contest in 1990 with Massachusetts’ Cambridge Center for Behavioral Studies as a standard Turing test: each judge held typed conversations with a program and a person at once and tried to tell which was which, and $1,500 and a bronze medal went to its most human-seeming program that first year, $2,000 in later years. Early rounds restricted questioning to one topic of each entrant’s choice, such as whimsical conversation, which suited standard chatbot tricks; discussion became unrestricted from 1995. It was reported defunct as of 2020.

loebner-prize-1991.detail:
Two larger prizes were never awarded. $25,000 awaited the first program that judges could not distinguish from a human while believing the human was the computer, and $100,000 awaited one passing a Turing test including text, visual and auditory input, after which competition was to end. Interactions were originally as brief as 2.5 minutes.

Marvin Minsky offered a “prize” to anyone who could stop it, and Loebner replied that this made Minsky, in effect, co-sponsor. From 2014 AISB organised it at Bletchley Park, and its final 2019 edition dropped judging panels in favour of public votes with no human competitors.

lotus-marketplace-1991.summary: In January 1991 Lotus cancelled a CD-ROM profiling 120 million Americans after 30,000 people wrote to object and asked to have their information removed. Announced on April 10, 1990, it would have put data on those people in 80 million U.S. households onto desktop computers whose owners could export names for unrestricted use. Protest spread through computer conferences and bulletin boards after a November 1990 Wall Street Journal story; cancellation came on January 23, 1991.

sources.title: Lotus cancels database product on privacy concerns - UPI
The Lessons of the Lotus MarketPlace
COMPANY NEWS; New Data Base Ended By Lotus and ...

lotus-marketplace-1991.detail:
That Macintosh product sorted households into about 50 neighbourhood types, and buyers controlled its disc outright. Lotus president Jim Manzi said his company “couldn't ignore the high level of consumer concern,” and their joint statement cited “the substantial, unexpected additional costs required to fully address consumer privacy issues” as well; Lotus spokeswoman Janice Brown estimated $2 million yearly for a phone line handling corrections and removals plus a public-relations campaign. Equifax supplied data from its Consumer Marketing Database. Product manager Robert Hilles said lifestyle groups such as “movers and shakers” and “difficult times” were not specific to individuals, could contain as few as 10 to 15 households, and held no buying-habit or credit-history data. Its companion Lotus MarketPlace: Business, already on sale with 7 million businesses, was cancelled too.

Culnan’s paper for 1991’s Computers, Freedom and Privacy conference called that episode “the new age of the electronic grassroots lobbyist,” noting that desktop products lacked mailing-list brokers’ screening and decoy-name controls.

mexico-city-seismic-alert-system-1991.summary: After a 1985 earthquake killed thousands in Mexico City, Centro de Instrumentación y Registro Sísmico (CIRES), a non-profit engineering group, built Sistema de Alerta Sísmica. Twelve accelerometer stations along Guerrero's coast, 300 kilometres from Mexico City, detect a large rupture and radio an alert that arrives about 60 seconds before strong shaking arrives, since radio waves outrun seismic waves. Public operation began in August 1991 with alerts broadcast on commercial radio stations, then on dedicated receivers in schools and metro stations. Its first large public warning came for a Copala earthquake on 14 September 1995. Juan Manuel Espinosa-Aranda's team published its design in 1995; no other major city then had a public earthquake warning system.

mexico-city-seismic-alert-system-1991.detail: Expanded as SASMEX with stations in Oaxaca and other states, this network sounded sirens across Mexico City on 7 September 2017, giving about two minutes' warning, but gave only seconds on 19 September 2017 because that quake began close to Mexico City. Japan's UrEDAS protected railways from 1992 and its nationwide public system followed in 2007.

param-8000-supercomputer-1991.summary: After United States refused India a Cray XMP for weather modelling in 1987, Government of India set up Centre for Development of Advanced Computing in Pune under Vijay Bhatkar in 1988. By 1991 its team delivered PARAM 8000, a distributed memory machine of 64 Inmos transputers in a reconfigurable network, with its own parallel programming environment, benchmarked near one gigaflop. Shown at a Zurich supercomputing exhibition in 1991, it was sold to Russia, Germany and Canada and copied in later PARAM generations through PARAM 10000 in 1998. C-DAC trained parallel programmers across Indian institutes and seeded a national supercomputing mission.

sources.title: Vijay P. Bhatkar, 'PARAM parallel supercomputer: architecture, programming environment, and applications', Proceedings of 8th International Parallel Processing Symposium (IEEE, 1994)
sources.author: Vijay P. Bhatkar
sources.confirms: PARAM architecture, transputer nodes, programming environment

pgp-1991.summary: In June 1991 Phil Zimmermann released PGP, strong encryption for anyone's email; the government investigated him for three years, then quit. PGP (Pretty Good Privacy) encrypts and signs texts, e-mails and files, giving privacy and proof of who sent them; Zimmermann, a long-time anti-nuclear activist, wrote it so people like him could use bulletin boards and store messages securely. Copies spread abroad, and in February 1993 he became the target of a US criminal investigation for “munitions export without a license,” closed without charges in 1996.

sources.title: Asset split
Zimmermann, Philip, 'PGP Marks 30th Anniversary', 6 June 2021
sources.author: Zimmermann, Philip
sources.confirms: PGP 1.0 was released on 6 June 1991 and a three-year US criminal investigation followed before being dropped in 1996.

sources.title: Markoff, John. 'Data-Secrecy Export Case Dropped by U.S.' New York Times, 12 January 1996.
sources.author: John Markoff
sources.confirms: Reports that the Justice Department dropped its three-year investigation of Zimmermann over PGP, which he had placed on the internet in spring 1991.

pgp-1991.detail:
Zimmermann sent it to Allan Hoeltje, who posted it to Peacenet, an ISP for political activists, and to Kelly Goen, who uploaded it to a Usenet source-code newsgroup. Zimmermann was unsure whether online postings began June 5 or 6. He charged no fee for non-commercial use and included full source code. PGP’s name came from “Ralph's Pretty Good Grocery” in Garrison Keillor’s fictional Lake Wobegon, and its first version used BassOmatic, a symmetric-key cipher of Zimmermann’s own design named after a Saturday Night Live sketch. Goen marked his Usenet post “US only” at Zimmermann’s request and also uploaded it to many bulletin boards; Zimmermann later wrote that he had not known such tags were merely advisory.

Under US export rules then in force, cryptosystems with keys larger than 40 bits counted as munitions, and PGP never used keys smaller than 128 bits. In 1995 Zimmermann published PGP’s complete source code as a hardback through MIT Press so anyone abroad could scan its pages and compile it, relying on First Amendment protection for book exports; courts never tested that question for PGP. In 1995 cryptographer Bruce Schneier called an early version “the closest you're likely to get to military-grade encryption.”

pinatubo-eruption-forecast-1991.summary: After Mount Pinatubo on Luzon stirs in April 1991, Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology and a US Geological Survey team install seismometers, tiltmeters and a correlation spectrometer that records soaring sulfur dioxide. A five-level alert scheme, a video on pyroclastic flows and hazard maps persuade local officials and Clark Air Base commanders to act. More than 60,000 people are moved before 15 June, when Pinatubo ejects about five cubic kilometres of material in a century's largest eruption. USGS estimates at least 5,000 lives and 250 million dollars in property saved; about 850 people still died, many under ash-laden roofs collapsing in Typhoon Yunya's rain.

python-1991.summary: In 1991 Guido van Rossum posted Python 0.9.0, a language built to be read, with version 1.0 following in 1994; it became the language of data science and AI. He had conceived it in the late 1980s at Centrum Wiskunde & Informatica (CWI) in the Netherlands as ABC’s successor and began implementing it in December 1989, naming it after the British comedy series Monty Python’s Flying Circus. Python emphasises readable code through significant indentation, its “batteries-included” standard library and garbage collection. Van Rossum led its development as “benevolent dictator for life” until 12 July 2018; a five-member Steering Council was elected in January 2019.

van Rossum, Guido, Python Reference Manual, CWI Report CS-R9525

sources.venue: Centrum voor Wiskunde en Informatica, Amsterdam

sources.title: 'Python', Encyclopaedia Britannica

python-1991.verification_note: Britannica dates Python's development to 1991 but its public release to 1994, version 1.0's year; a 1991 release refers to version 0.9.0's posting.
python-1991.detail:
Python is dynamically typed and supports several programming styles. ABC, inspired by SETL, handled exceptions and interfaced with the Amoeba operating system. Python 2.0 arrived on 16 October 2000 with list comprehensions, cycle-detecting garbage collection, reference counting and Unicode support. Python 3.0 in 2008 was a major revision not fully backward-compatible with earlier versions, and Python 2.7’s end of life was postponed from 2015 to 2020 because so much existing code could not easily be ported; it no longer receives security patches. From Python 3.5 the language added optional static typing.

Python is widely taught as an introductory programming language. As of 2026 the Python Software Foundation supports versions 3.11 through 3.15, all given expedited security releases in October 2026.

rhodes-ip-link-1991.summary: At 10:44 on 12 November 1991, Mike Lawrie's team at Rhodes University in Grahamstown exchanged packets with Randy Bush's host in Portland, Oregon over a leased line, giving South African universities a direct TCP/IP connection. Email had reached Rhodes via FidoNet dial-up since 1989 under UniNet, an academic network that evaded Telkom's monopoly through a common-interest exemption. Telkom at first refused an international line for carrying 'third-party traffic', and sanctions kept US agencies from funding. Within two years TICSA sold the first commercial accounts, and Internet access spread from campuses to South African business and homes.

Earlier, Rhodes staff Dave Wilson and Mike Lawrie had run a FidoNet store-and-forward gateway through Randy Bush's home system, and UniNet relayed email across South African universities over X.25. semipalatinsk-test-site-closed-1991.summary: Soviet weapons designers detonate their first atomic bomb on 29 August 1949 at a steppe polygon west of Semipalatinsk, and over forty years conduct 456 tests there, 116 in atmosphere or at surface before 1963 and 340 underground, exposing herders and townspeople downwind in Kazakh villages to fallout. A 1989 underground test vents gas, and poet Olzhas Suleimenov founds Nevada-Semipalatinsk, a mass movement that gathers a million signatures and forces cancellation of 11 of 18 tests planned that year. Nursultan Nazarbayev, president of a Kazakhstan still inside a collapsing union, signs Decree 409 on 29 August 1991 closing the polygon. Kazakhstan then gives up 1,400 inherited warheads, and the UN later marks 29 August as International Day against Nuclear Tests.

south-africa-nuclear-dismantling-1991.summary: In November 1989 F. W. de Klerk's government halted weapons production, and on 26 February 1990 he ordered destruction of six completed gun-type devices and a partly built seventh. ARMSCOR's Circle facility near Pelindaba dismantled them in secret; by 6 September 1991 all highly enriched uranium had been removed, melted down and returned to South Africa's Atomic Energy Corporation. South Africa joined the Non-Proliferation Treaty on 10 July 1991 and signed a full-scope safeguards agreement on 16 September. De Klerk disclosed everything to parliament on 24 March 1993, after which IAEA teams checked uranium inventories and dismantled facilities. No other state has built nuclear weapons and then verifiably given them up.

southern-cone-chagas-initiative-1991.summary: In July 1991 health ministers of Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Chile, Paraguay and Uruguay, meeting in Brasília under PAHO auspices, agreed to eliminate domestic populations of Triatoma infestans, main vector of Trypanosoma cruzi, and to screen all blood donations. Teams sprayed millions of houses with pyrethroid insecticides, communities reported re-infestation, and blood banks adopted serological screening. Uruguay was certified free of vector transmission in 1997, Chile in 1999 and Brazil in 2006; estimated new infections across the region fell by more than 70 percent during the 1990s, and incidence in children dropped sharply. The initiative became a model for parallel programmes in Andean and Central American countries and showed how coordinated vector control could suppress a parasitic disease of poor rural housing.

sources.title: Dias, João Carlos Pinto; Silveira, Antonio Carlos; Schofield, Chris J., 'The impact of Chagas disease control in Latin America: a review', Memórias do Instituto Oswaldo Cruz 97, no. 5 (2002)

sources.confirms: 1991 launch, house spraying, blood screening, certification of Uruguay 1997 and Chile 1999, decline in incidence.

sources.author: Schofield, C. J.; Dias, J. C. P.
sources.confirms: Entomological basis, programme structure and early results.

southern-cone-chagas-initiative-1991.detail: Dias, Silveira and Schofield's review in Memórias do Instituto Oswaldo Cruz gives programme design, costs and certification dates; Schofield and Dias's earlier Advances in Parasitology chapter sets out entomological basis. Sylvatic T. infestans foci in Bolivia complicate final elimination. Chagas disease then infected an estimated 16 to 18 million people and threatened 100 million; vector lives in cracks of adobe and thatch houses. Brazil's programme had sprayed since 1975, and Argentina since 1960s, but coordination addressed re-invasion across borders. Argentina's certification followed in several provinces; Bolivia and Paraguay progressed later. Blood screening coverage rose from under 50 percent to near 100 percent.
